Name: Alex Johnston
Question: How would you rate the musicianship of jazz legend Charlie Parker? Does his legacy stand up even today with so many talented people playing now?
Answer: You can tell the history of jazz in four words: Louis Armstrong, Charlie Parker. —Miles Davis Hi. Welcome to this answer. Please make yourself comfortable. We have some ground to cover. (Photo by William P. Gottlieb, source: [Portrait of Charlie Parker, Three Deuces, New York, N.Y., ca. Aug. 1947]) The Bare Minimum of Largely Unedifying Facts in the Case of Charles Parker Jr. Charlie Parker was born in Kansas City, Kansas, on August 29, 1920. His father Charles Sr was a dancer and singer and a serious alcoholic, and his mother Addie wouldn’t tolerate alcohol in the house. His parents separated, Charles Sr eventually becoming a chef on Pullman cars, which took him off around the country. Charles Jr began playing alto saxophone at the age of 11, but wasn’t very good at it. His mother bought him a new sax when he was 14, and he joined his high school band. In his mid-teens, he began to take music more seriously, and was taught the basics of improvisation by a local musician, trombonist Robert Simpson. Around this time, when he was first playing out as a musician, he got introduced to drugs. The same year, Parker proposed to his girlfriend, Rebecca Ruffin, and they were married. Again in 1936, on the way to a gig, he was in a car crash in which he broke three ribs. His effort to manage the pain may well have got him more dependent upon opioids. By 1937 he was addicted to heroin. At some point around this period, he adopted a regimen of practicing for several hours a day. He would sometimes vanish for days, because he was off practicing. His mother would go and find him and bring him home, he’d eat like a horse and then sleep for a couple of days, and then do it all over again. By 1937 he was working as a professional musician, actively seeking gigs. A residency in the Ozarks gave him ample practice time. In 1938 he joined Jay McShann’s band. In 1939 he went to New York City, where he worked for several months at several jobs, including dishwasher and washing cars. He was still practicing incessantly and playing at every opportunity he could find. His drug use slackened off, because he couldn’t afford them. All through his adult life, Parker alternated between being relatively clean, and using heroin. In 1940, he learned that his father had been stabbed to death. He returned to Kansas City for the funeral and rejoined Jay McShann’s band. While on tour with McShann he was introduced to Dizzy Gillespie, a trumpet player who was then with Cab Calloways’ orchestra. In 1942 Parker left McShann’s band and joined that of Earl Hines, a veteran pianist who’d played on many of Louis Armstrong’s classic early recordings. Here he played with Gillespie regularly for the first time: Gillespie had been fired from Calloway’s band after a misunderstanding that had led to a fight. In 1942, the American Federation of Musicians instituted a recording strike that would last until 1944. Parker left McShann’s band and started hanging out in New York with the group of musicians that centred around regular jam sessions in places like Minton’s Playhouse and Monroe’s Uptown House. (I wrote about this period in Alex Johnston's answer to What is Bebop in Jazz music?) The musicians at these sessions included Gillespie, pianist and composer Thelonious Monk, drummer Kenny Clarke, pianist Bud Powell, bassist Oscar Pettiford, and others. (Miles Davis joined the scene later on.) But these were not the only musicians who had been working towards taking jazz in a new direction, away from the riff-based swing that was then the dominant form of popular music in the Western world. Lots of other musicians had grown tired of swing and were pushing for something new. (This is amply documented in Gitler: see Sources.) It was into this situation that Parker arrived, having already made contact with Gillespie. He was almost immediately recognised by his peers as the dominant figure in the new music. From 1942 onwards, Parker, Gillespie and their colleagues made the first recordings of a new kind of jazz that would later be dubbed ‘bebop’, sometimes to the annoyance of the musicians themselves. Parker and Gillespie made many recordings together. In late 1946, Parker’s drug use became uncontrollable. He was asleep one night at the Civic Hotel when he accidentally set light to his mattress. He was arrested, beaten and jailed, then was checked into Camarillo State Hospital for six months. He got out in spring 1947, clean and healthy, and made dozens of recordings for the Savoy and Dial labels, with a band featuring Davis on trumpet and Max Roach on drums. For the next few years he continued to make the studio and live recordings which are the foundation of his legacy. He loved classical music, and made an album with a string section which was his most popular recording in his lifetime. He became tired of the limitations of three-minute recordings and song- and blues-based forms, and approached the modernist composer Edgard Varèse for music lessons. But he also went back to using drugs. When he wasn’t on drugs, he often drank to excess. At some point (I haven’t been able to find out when) he divorced his first wife Rebecca, married again (Doris) and divorced again, and then met his third and last partner Chan Richardson, with whom he had a daughter, Pree. Pree died in 1954 and Parker never got over her death. He attempted suicide twice and separated from Chan. In March 1955, he was at the apartment of his friend Nica de Koenigswarter, watching TV, when he had a heart attack and died. He was only 34 years old. The coroner who performed the autopsy had no idea of his birthdate, and estimated his age as being between 50 and 60. He is buried in Kansas City. For many years, his gravestone had the wrong date of death: March 23 instead of March 12. This was eventually fixed in 1992. However, the replacement gravestone bears an image of a tenor saxophone. Charlie Parker did not play the tenor sax. Not as his main instrument, anyway. His principal instrument was alto sax. Such were the fortunes of a jazz musician in the mid-20th century. Like so many lives of mid-20th century African-American jazz musicians, when you spell out the bare externals of Charlie Parker’s life like that, it’s mostly depressing. But what that story doesn’t tell you is what his impact was like on other people. What it was like to be around him. What people thought of him. You see, the opinions about Parker’s musicianship that truly matter, are not mine. What matters is the testimony of people who really knew his music, and understood from the inside what he was doing, and what made him different. Charlie Parker grew up in Kansas City. If we were to list only three cities in the USA which deserve to be regarded as true cradles of jazz, the first would be New Orleans, where jazz was created in the first place. The second would be New York City, where most great jazz musicians in the early/mid 20th century ended up coming to. The third would be Kansas City. In jazz terms, it was an astonishing combination of boot camp, battlefield and nursery. Stanley Crouch brilliantly describes Kansas City’s music scene in what I think is the best single book about Parker thus far for the general reader, Kansas City Lightning. Charlie Parker came out of Kansas City as one of those musicians who soaks up music more easily than other musicians do. When he was first living in New York in 1939, he attended a jam session at Dan Wall’s Chili House on Seventh Avenue and 140th Street, presided over by guitarist William ‘Biddy’ Fleet. Fleet noticed that Parker was interested in doing something unusual, and the thing that he really liked about Parker was that he didn’t need to go off and practice new ideas in privacy. He seemed to be able to absorb them instantly. His dexterity and the power of his playing became notorious. Many older sax players held their saxes at an angle in imitation of another of Parker’s influences, Lester Young, or otherwise posed while they played, or closed their eyes. Parker held his straight, and stared directly ahead while playing, and didn’t move, which earned him another nickname: Indian, after the wooden advertising figures used by tobacconists. During jam sessions among his friends, if things were getting competitive, someone would say ‘Go get Indian’, and Parker would be summoned from wherever he was practicing so that he could blow the interloper off the stage. His clean, aggressive tone makes his music stand out, especially on his many live recordings, where the rest of the band is sometimes a murky sound in the middle distance but he’s always there, in the foreground, his sax leaping up to the treble and then finding the most intricate and exploratory route down again. The jazz scholar Thomas Owens noted that Parker often accentuates the highest note in any phrase, and that’s one of the things that gives his playing that sense of soaring freedom, which in turn is why the nickname ‘Bird’ stuck to him. There are loads of stories about Parker’s negative personal habits: his tendency to pawn other people’s stuff so he could get money for drugs; his chronic lateness; his general unreliability as a human being; his greed (Miles Davis complains at length about this in his autobiography); his fatal susceptibility to his own appetites, which is maybe the same thing. There’s no getting around the fact that Parker as a human being was one of the legendary fuck-ups of jazz. The strange thing is that he’s not the kind of musician whose music was about how messed up he was. He’s not a Lester Young, or a Chet Baker, whose music seems to have functioned as a balm to their souls, a consolation for all the crap that they put up with. Parker’s tone is bright, aggressive and immensely confident. His music surges with life and power. It bucks you up. What was it like to be around that? The Testimonials It was one of the greatest uplifts of my life. Men like that just lift you up. It wouldn’t matter if they were playing with a washboard. They would still sound good. —Art Blakey, on the experience of playing with Charlie Parker It’s rare to get a genius on the scene. I guess not more than one will come along every quarter-century in any field you can think of. But Bird had all the necessary equipment. You could just follow the leader as far as Charlie Parker was concerned. —Kenny Clarke In my opinion, Bud (Powell) was a genius just like Bird. They were untouchable as far as their musicianship was concerned. They could do no wrong in anything they did, which was a hell of a mark for a young cat to try to achieve. —Sonny Rollins Bird used to come to Minton’s, and he was so great that everyone would leave the bandstand when he played. All the bad saxophone players showed him respect and let him have the bandstand. —Kenny Dorham The thing about Charlie Parker was that he was such a giant. He was so much better than everybody else. It’s not like there was this guy and that guy. There was everybody else, and there was Charlie. —Al Cohn [Parker] was always reading and learning. He was a very educated man. He could talk about—my car was goofing off and I said ‘Damn! I’m going to take this thing to the garage,’ and he said, ‘It ain’t nothin’ but such-and-such,’ and he got out there, and he went around the motor, and he fixed the damn thing! He knew all about the motor and what caused it to run and all that shit. He educated me to a lot of things because I’d go and keep him company. I know he’s over there by himself; he wasn’t interested in girls. Nothing they could do for him. He was outta sight. We used to sit up and listen to Firebird Suite and Rite of Spring. He hipped me to Stravinsky. ’Cause I wasn’t listening to that. I was listening to arrangers and bands. I wasn’t paying much attention to this real serious side of music, but he educated me to that fact and made me listen to it. And I got to learn Bartok and Wagner and all those guys. —Howard McGhee To me a Charlie Parker composition is a classic, it’s a work of art! —Freddie Hubbard Playing with Bird was an experience. Every night he would put something new in the tunes we played, like changing chords, playing different progressions. You never felt that you had to play the same thing you had played the night before. We used to wail! That’s what I dig. It was one of my greatest experiences; his mind was so fast. Other than playing the saxophone, Charlie was a very brilliant man. —Errol Garner Yard [Parker] was without a doubt my very favorite musician of all time. My favorite musician now is Dizzy. But Yard, I still hear things of his today that are so phenomenal I don’t believe it. […] In my estimation no-one has caught up with this man. —Carmen McRae You'll see that if Charlie Parker wanted to invoke plagiarism laws, he could sue almost anyone who's made a record in the last 10 years. If I were Bird, I've have all the best boppers in the country thrown into jail. —Lennie Tristano My uncle played me a Charlie Parker record when I was ten. I hated it—like hating your first cigarette, and then twenty years later you’re on twenty a day. —Derek Bailey I learned about improvising from Bean, Monk, Don Byas, Lucky Thompson and Bird. But Bird was such a great and inventive improviser that he would turn songs inside out. If you didn’t know music, you didn’t know where the fuck Bird was at when he was improvising. See, Bean, Don Byas, Lucky Thompson all had the same style: they would run their solos and then they would improvise. You could still hear the melody when they improvised. But when Bird played, it was totally another ball game, totally something else, something different every time. Among masters he was the master. —Miles Davis What did Charlie Parker do? He was no child prodigy. Bud Powell started piano lessons at five, and was playing in his brother William’s band at the age of 15. Parker’s early life, by contrast, has two famous moments of public humiliation. On one occasion, he went to a practice session of local musicians, at a time when he only knew how to play two songs, and not all of one of them: Fats Waller’s ‘Honeysuckle Rose’, and the first half of Hoagy Carmichael’s ‘Lazy River’ in F. The group started to play ‘Body and Soul’, and Parker was mortified, because he didn’t know it. He went off, determined to learn as many songs in as many keys as possible. Another time, around 1936, he attended one of Kansas City’s notoriously cutthroat jam sessions. Behind the drum kit at this session was one of the town’s top musicians: Count Basie’s drummer, Jo Jones. Parker started to play, but he lost track of the rhythm. Bass player Gene Ramey, who was there that night, observed that he was ahead of the rest of the band. Jo Jones had a way of signalling to a player that his time was up: he would hit the bell of his ride cymbal. He hit it, but Parker didn’t notice. He hit it again. People in the crowd were starting to say ‘Get this cat off of here.’ So Jones took his cymbal off its stand and dropped it on the floor. Everyone laughed, except 16-year-old Charlie Parker, who stopped playing and left the bandstand. He went back to stand with Ramey and others. Ramey advised him to ‘stop playing like you’re so anxious, because if you’re so anxious like that you’re sure to get ahead of them.’ ‘It’s all right,’ Parker said, keeping his face as impassive as possible to mask his frustration, and then he added, rather like the Terminator, ‘I’ll be back.’ More than one Parker biographer has noted that there was an element in his makeup of wanting to be never at a loss. His legendary practice regimen, which began some time in the mid-30s and ended around the time he properly hit the New York scene around 1942, was focused around learning as many things as possible in as many keys as possible, so that he could never be caught out again, the way he was at that practice session where he only knew one and a half songs. I’m not a sax player, so I don’t understand the arcane specifics of sax fingering, but whereas it’s relatively easy to transpose tunes on the guitar (shift your hand up and down the neck, bingo), it’s different with wind instruments. Parker formed his playing style so that he could never again get lost on his instrument, the way he did at those jam sessions as a teenager. When, in 1946, he recorded a version of ‘Lover Man’ while badly strung out and suffering from malnutrition, you can hear him playing in uncharacteristically short-breathed, broken phrases. It’s clearly the sound of a great musician in a very bad way. (It was later that night when the mattress-on-fire incident happened.) The recording was issued, and some people love it, but he was furious about it. It wasn’t his sound, the way he wanted to be heard. Inasmuch as he wanted always to be in full command of what he was doing, Charlie Parker was unlike John Coltrane. The jazz critic Ben Ratliff noted that Coltrane was always at his most creative at times when he expressed uncertainty about what he was doing, and where he was going. Coltrane was an obsessive student: he was always trying to move on and learn more. Parker, by contrast, hated not knowing what he was doing. He was about overcoming musical problems with apparently effortless mastery. He, too, was a student: in 1954 he told a novice player You see, once you stop wantin’ to learn things, you’re not alive anymore. But he didn’t like to play when he felt unsure of himself. He presented himself as one who, as they say, had authority. Parker did not single-handedly invent bebop. He worked and worked his way to a place where he could soak up new influences instantly, and transform them into something that was his own. It has been noted many times that a lot of musicians, when they improvise, use formulas: riffs and licks that they’ve practiced and which they insert where appropriate, rather than make up something totally new each time. Most musicians, especially in rock music, have maybe a dozen or so of these. The jazz scholar Thomas Owens estimated that Parker had about a hundred of them. Owens’ book Bebop: The Music and its Players is a survey of the music divided into different instruments, but Parker is the only musician to have a chapter to himself, ‘The Parker Style’. He came along when musicians like Gillespie, Monk and Clarke had been working their way towards something new. They had been reworking jazz from the ground up, harmonically and rhythmically: Gillespie with his close study of harmony, Monk with his extremely individual style of composition. Charlie Parker came along, took the music and, because he had already figured out so much of it by himself, showed them what could be done with it. Sax players before Parker used a wide variety of expressive effects, such as Ben Webster’s fondness for emphasising the sound of his own breath, or Johnny Hodges’ exceptionally wide vibrato and bent notes. Parker didn’t use these effects. He didn’t try to vocalise with his sax, or seduce the listener with sexy glissandi. He himself described what he was doing as: I’m looking for the pretty notes. He wanted his music to be expressive in terms of the notes he played, not so much how he played them. And I think this is fundamental to his importance as a musician, because it’s one reason why he was so influential. You can transcribe a Parker solo, and get down almost all the important musical information in the form of notation. Parker’s hard tone and brief vibrato is less important than his phrasing, his note choices, his sense of the blues, his incredible, dazzling sense of musical logic. But if you were to transcribe a Johnny Hodges solo, or a solo by Ben Webster, it’d be a lot harder to indicate with notation what’s so effective about it. The jazz scholar Gunther Schuller transcribed Louis Armstrong’s brilliant unaccompanied intro to ‘West End Blues’ in his essential book Early Jazz, but then added the caveat that his transcription was really only an attempt to convey what Armstrong had played. Parker’s approach changed the music that was played, more than it changed the way the music was played. He didn’t just find a new way of playing what was already there. Just as Shakespeare expanded the English language, Charlie Parker expanded the language of jazz. Owens: [L]ying beneath the surface of his improvisations is another factor that helps generate the sense of rightness in his music. Typically entire phrases, and even entire choruses and groupings of choruses, are goal-oriented: they arrive on a final note that lies at the end of a length stepwise descent. Parker, through his huge effort of striving to understand where the music could go next, mastered the new direction, and made it seem natural and inevitable. He helped give jazz a new life. In another answer, I wrote about the cultural legacy of jazz being the improvisational attitude, the wily, skilful presence of mind required to overcome difficulties that have been placed in your way. Jazz music specialises in this: creating a harmonic and rhythmic labyrinth from which the musician must heroically escape. How the musician escapes from it creates what we think of as the musician’s style. Miles Davis didn’t so much escape the labyrinth as act as if it wasn’t a problem. In his earliest years he tried to sound like a more virtuosic player, such as Dizzy Gillespie, one of the greatest musicians in jazz history. He later developed a more low-key, insouciant style that floats around the harmony, alluding to it but not chained to it. (In the legendary Plugged Nickel recordings, Miles and his band challenged themselves to do the exact opposite, and the result is amazing, but he didn’t stick with that approach for long.) Miles would go on to devise one labyrinth after another, and in each case saunter through them with the same inimitable, electrifying cool. Other players have different ways of getting out of the labyrinth. John Coltrane used every tool in the toolbox to blast his way out, even calling upon god to help him. His music is heroic in its determination, and it’s always relentlessly serious, and if we love it, it’s partly because we’re always rooting for him. Chet Baker lies on his bunk in his cell, mourning his plight, having failed to notice that his cell door is actually unlocked. Charles Mingus’ labyrinth is also his fortress, with himself standing on the battlements, heckling society through a megaphone. Parker surveyed the labyrinth, assessed its weaknesses, rebuilt it to make it more difficult to escape, and then gave that wide-eyed, radiant smirk of his, the one you can see in the picture at the top of this answer. Then he soared upwards into freedom. That’s why it makes so little sense to talk of his ‘musicianship’, as if he were like any other jazz musician that comes along, in any generation. It’s like talking about whether or not Rembrandt could paint people so that they looked like themselves. If there are curious readers of this answer who’ve never actually heard Charlie Parker play, well, props to you for getting this far. And you’re probably wondering what all the fuss is about. Rather than lament the shortness of his life and the sadness of his early death, you ought to be rewarded with a blast of his music at its most powerful and exhilarating. And given that Parker credited Ray Noble’s ‘Cherokee’ as the tune that prompted his great musical breakthrough, we should finish on the tune Parker wrote over the chord changes to ‘Cherokee’: ‘Ko-Ko’. Charlie Parker was born on August 29, 1920. I posted this answer on this site on August 29, 2020. One hundred years later, to the day. Happy birthday, sir. And thank you. (Charlie Parker in a photo booth, Kansas City, 1940.) And thank you, reader, for your time. Sources:

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Out of all the conquests in human history, European colonization always seems to receive the most criticism. Was there anything uniquely bad about European imperialism, or is it simply a matter of scale and/or recency?
Answer: It’s because, if we are Europeans, and we wish to criticise colonialism, it is morally imperative that we criticise our own, before we criticise anyone else’s. I find it depressing that this basic lesson in ethics needs to be taught to, presumably, an adult, but there you go.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: What does Alex Johnston think of the band Soundgarden?
Answer: How nice to have a bespoke question. Normally, when I like a band, I like most of their stuff; some albums or phases more than others, but Soundgarden are unusual for me because, while I really love one of their albums—like, it’s possibly my favourite rock album of the 90s—I don’t care at all for the rest of their stuff. Why this should be, I don’t know. But I checked it recently, by having a quick listen to all the stuff I hadn’t listened to, or had listened to and not liked, and I felt the same: mild impatience (Soundgarden songs tend to take a while to get going), alternating with lack of interest. Which brings us to: Superunknown, from 1994. If Superunknown is simultaneously more focused and more stylistically diverse than other Soundgarden albums, I attribute some of this to its producer, Michael Beinhorn, who was active in this space up until a couple of years ago, and who I actually knew of before I listened to this album, because as a teenager I’d listened to Memory Serves by Material, the band Beinhorn had been in before he’d become a producer. I think Beinhorn was the perfect guy to guide Soundgarden towards making a masterpiece. Because I think Superunknown is a masterpiece, one of the great albums of the 90s. Confession: since we’re talking 90s bands, and grunge, I never really liked Nirvana. I disliked what I thought was the whiny tone of their songs. Or maybe it was just the sound of Cobain’s voice. Chris Cornell in Soundgarden also suffered from depression, and sadly it got him in the end, but Soundgarden never sound ‘whiny’, at least not on this album. This album delivered what I want from a hard rock album, because it’s all about power and confidence and swagger, without being boneheadedly phallic. (Heh heh: I said ‘bone’.) When Chris Cornell opens up his throat and gives those mighty yells, it’s exhilarating. He may be singing about despair and alienation, but he sounds to me like he’s defying them, rather than being crushed by them. Very rarely for me with an album that straddles genres such as hard rock and metal, there are almost no songs on this that I routinely skip. I’ve probably been involuntarily subjected to ‘Black Hole Sun’ too many times, but it is a brilliantly written song, and very effective. For me, the outstanding tracks are the ones that have more of a groove. ‘Let Me Drown’ is a great track 1; so what if I don’t exactly know what it’s about? (I just read the lyrics for the first time, and I’m still not much the wiser.) ‘My Wave’ has that guitar hook in the chorus, which always made me think of R.E.M. in a good way. ‘Fell On Black Days’ is a little on the nose, for me, and ‘Mailman’ is a bit of a plodder, but then we get into the title track, with that blistering jangly riff: a song which to me is about the experience of listening to the album of which it’s the title track. And the chorus is a real belter, with that cool minor-second riff. That’s why I love this album. Well, that and the deeply odd next track, Ben Shepherd’s ‘Head Down’, which sounds like a small acoustic band close by playing along with a far louder, heavily amplified rock monster in the distance. Dreamy, doomy, sly, trippy, magnificent. I saw the video for ‘Spoonman’ a lot back then, and Cornell was right when he remarked that the band was clever to keep out of it. Instead, it’s mostly the titular character doing his thing: the band appears only in pictures. This gave them a certain mystique, although when you did glimpse them, they were intriguingly ragbag: L to r: Kim Thayil, Ben Shepherd, Chris Cornell, Matt Cameron; or, the Beardy Indian One, Lyle Lovett, the Rock God and the Kid Brother of the Surfer. ‘Spoonman’, like ‘My Wave’ mixes up time signatures: the main riff is in 7/4, the chorus is in 4/4 and during Artis’ spoons solo it drops into 3/4. That keeps things lurching along in an interesting way. Then there’s the jaunty shanty of ‘Limo Wreck’, and we’re into another angsty ballad, ‘The Day I Tried to Live’. I admit to being very tempted to skip this one. After that, there’s a brief burst of pure punk rock with ‘Kickstand’ and then we’re into the majestic ‘Fresh Tendrils’, featuring the ominous clavinet of Natasha Shneider. I didn’t realise until a few years later that I had fallen briefly in crush with Natasha Shneider after seeing her in Peter Hyams’ 1984 movie 2010, where she played a young cosmonaut opposite Roy Scheider and Helen Mirren: Anyway: RIP, Ms Shneider. (She died of cancer in 2008, aged only 52.) Your hammering clavinet is a big part of why this song is so great. ‘Fresh Tendrils’ fulfils all my requirements for a great rock song: it sounds awesome, and it’s opaque enough that I can project my own interpretation onto it. And it’s written by the drummer. Then we’re onto ‘4th of July’, a more sardonic ballad than the other ones, which is maybe why I generally prefer it—even if I concede that it’s not, like ‘Black Hole Sun’ is, a song that could be covered by Frank Sinatra and still sound great. (Paul Anka did cover ‘Black Hole Sun’ on Rock Swings and the result is mostly as grisly as the rest of that sorry exercise in painfully heterosexual camp.) There’s another Shepherd song, the weird ‘Half’, and then the official final track, ‘Like Suicide’, which I always admired for its music but otherwise disliked for what I thought was its romanticisation of human damage—until very recently, when I realised it’s literally Chris Cornell writing about a bird that flew into a window of his house, whereupon my regard for it skyrocketed. An epic, slow-build hard rock song about a dead bird. Amazing. After being wrung out by ‘Like Suicide’, I seldom had the energy for the throwaway bonus track that appeared on my international CD, ‘She Likes Surprises’. I definitely liked Superunknown in part because I was the right kind of listener for it: about 23–24, young, dumb, frustrated and at least somewhat alienated. (I was, at the time, 2–3 years into the long stretch between my first girlfriend and my second one.) For all the nihilism and despair, it was crackling with energy and life. And it still bucks me up, with its odd, irregular metres and sexy riffs, and moments of lightness and dream. And what other great rock album has a.) a song about a dead bird, b.) a song you could imagine being arranged by Gordon Jenkins, and c.) a f***ing spoons solo? I faithfully bought Down on the Upside, but it was a headache. I was starting to move on from rock music. Still, if you can make one great album, that’s greatness enough. Ave atque vale, gentlemen. Edit: I’d like to dedicate this answer to the memory of another rock hero of mine, recently departed. RIP Steve Albini.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Is Jim Halpert a sociopath?
Answer: Not even slightly. Jim Halpert, non-sociopath I don’t trust dictionary definitions much, but as I understand sociopathy, it involves a lack of concern for society and ideas of right and wrong, and a lack of respect for the feelings of others. Jim has neither of these things. Yes, he likes to prank some people, but look at who he pranks: the two most annoying and overbearing people in his vicinity, Dwight and Andy. He pranks Dwight both to relieve his own boredom with his job (which job he does very well, even though he doesn’t work very hard) but mainly to puncture Dwight’s absurd pomposity. When he first pranks Andy, Andy explodes in a violent rage, and Jim—clearly aware that pranking Andy will have potentially worse consequences than pranking Dwight—doesn’t prank him again until much later, when Andy is being peak annoying. I’ve skimmed a couple of ‘Jim is a jerk/Jim is objectively a scumbag’ articles, and they are unconvincing. One article claimed in a subheading that Jim cheats on Pam, but then dialled it down in the text to observing that Jim has the opportunity to cheat on Pam: very shoddy journalism. This is of course a reference to Cathy, who blatantly attempts to seduce Jim in Florida by showing up in his room in her pyjamas, and then goes further by taking a shower and lying on his bed in nothing but a bathrobe—and then has the nerve to act offended when Jim points out that he’s married. Jim takes numerous measures to get rid of her, and ultimately spends the night in Dwight’s room, eating desserts and watching sports with his usual rival. (In a deleted scene, Jim talks to Pam on the phone and flat-out tells her about the whole Cathy situation, which she finds both amusing and ‘pathetic’.) The producers actually wanted Jim to cheat on Pam with Cathy, but John Krasinski firmly refused. Jim and Pam’s marital problems were deferred until season 9, and his attempt to help start up the sports marketing company in Philadelphia: eventually he chooses to stop working for the startup, because it’s damaging his marriage. That is not the action of a sociopath. One common criticism of Jim is for the rather blunt way he breaks up with his girlfriend Katy in season 2’s ‘Booze Cruise’. Roy has just publicly announced a date for he and Pam to get married: Katy: Do you think that'll ever be us? Jim: No. Katy: What is wrong with you? Why did you even bring me here tonight? Jim: I don't know. Let's break up. Katy: Whoa. What? This happens at the very moment Jim realises that his love for Pam—which he came very close to confessing to her in the previous episode, ‘Christmas Party’—is doomed, because she’s finally going to get married. Under the circumstances, breaking up with the girlfriend he doesn't love is a highly honourable thing to do, even if he could have been more gentle about it (but this is funnier.) I mean, compare Andy, who in season 8 travels to Florida to win back Erin, and only on the trip home with her does he get around to breaking up with his existing girlfriend, Jessica. Another article observed that Jim pranks Dwight, but when Dwight pranks him back, in season 7’s ‘Classy Christmas’, he can’t handle it. This fails to note that Dwight’s prank is characteristically Dwight-ish in that Dwight goes way too far, relentlessly ambushing Jim with snowballs, and throwing them with such force that Jim gets a bloody nose. It goes on beyond the point where anyone except Dwight finds it funny. Jim’s pranks are never actually brutal. Who’s the sociopath now, entertainment news content providers? In season 4’s ‘Money’, Angela has broken off her relationship with Dwight because he euthanised her beloved cat without her permission (and rather clumsily, at that). Dwight is so heartbroken that he takes to sitting in the stairwell, moaning. Jim, who at this stage in the show still doesn’t really like Dwight, sits down next to him and says this: Did I ever tell you why I left Scranton? Yeah, I didn't think I had. Well, it was all about Pam. Yeah, I mean, she was with Roy... and I just couldn't take it. I mean, I lost it, Dwight. I couldn't sleep, I couldn't concentrate on anything. And then weird stuff, like, food had no taste. So my solution was to move away. It was awful. And it is something that I wouldn't wish on my worst enemy. And that includes you. Again, not the act of someone who lacks regard for other people’s feelings. Five seasons later, Jim and Dwight have buried the hatchet. One reason why is that Jim saved Dwight from getting fired. Dwight was going to take credit for the Sabre store, but Jim, alerted by Robert California, physically prevents Dwight from doing so, wrestling with him outside the conference room. Todd Packer steps in to do it, and duly gets canned. A stunned Dwight witnesses this, and wordlessly holds out his hand to Jim so he can get up from the floor. Their rivalry is effectively over, as of that point. In the penultimate episode of the final season, Dwight is regional manager, and Jim is not assistant regional manager but assistant to the regional manager. Dwight asks Jim for advice. Jim has been happily pranking Dwight all episode, by subtly manipulating Dwight into appointing himself as Jim’s assistant (prompting Dwight to remark with satisfaction From now on, anyone who needs to speak to me has got to go through me first). He first tries to palm Dwight off to his assistant (Dwight himself) but Dwight is serious: he plans to marry Esther, who is beautiful and young, plus ‘Her family admires me, my family tolerates hers’, and her dowry includes a walk-in freezer full of frozen premium cattle sperm. But the problem, Dwight admits, is Angela, who has a baby that Dwight thought his own, but the DNA test says otherwise. Jim’s advice is wise and heartfelt: Jim: I don't know what you want me to tell you, man. All I know is that every time I've been faced with a tough decision, there's only one thing that outweighs every other concern. One thing that will make you give up on everything you thought you knew, every instinct, every rational calculation. Dwight: Some sort of virus? Jim: Love. Dwight: Oh. Jim: Dwight, listen: no matter what happens, you gotta forget about all the other stuff. You gotta forget about logic and fear and doubt. You just gotta do everything you can to get to the one woman who's gonna make all this worth it. At the end of the day, you gotta jump. You love Angela, Dwight. I think you always have. Dwight: You're a good assistant, Jim. Jim: Not as good as you. Dwight: That's very true. Get the hell outta here. That’s not someone who doesn’t care for other people’s feelings. In the same episode, Pam has been worrying that Jim will always regret not pursuing the other job in Philadelphia. She confesses this to Jim, and he requests the documentary crew to cut together a DVD of scenes of Jim and Pam having moments of love. Pam watches this, much moved, whereupon Jim gives her the Christmas card he almost gave her in ‘Christmas Party’, in which card he first confessed his love to her. Back then, he’d decided not to give it to her, because she was engaged to Roy: he gives it to her now, seven years later, because it’s what she needs to hear from him. Jim understands right and wrong, and is willing to do small, relatively harmless wrongs, but he understands people enough and sympathises with them enough to do right by them when it matters. The ‘Jim is actually a jerk’ articles ignore all that. Jim Halpert is not a saint or a role model, just a happily married sports marketing exec and former paper salesman, living in Austin. And not a sociopath.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: What is your review of The Office (U.S. TV series)?
Answer: The main cast of The Office, US version, season 3, except for the black-haired woman at the back on the left, a minor supporting character who doesn’t really belong in this photo but I guess she was there on the day. I have a theory about the US version of The Office, which I think illuminates both versions, but which also might illuminate: It’s rather elaborate, though, so if you’re in a hurry, please bookmark this for reading later. Otherwise, get a beverage and take a seat. Let’s grab this thing and shake it until we get some results. … That’s what she said. One of the things that more recent American sitcoms have liked to do is show the characters growing. A situation is set up, things go wrong, there are amusing complications and after 24 or so minutes it winds up with what the creators of Seinfeld mocked as ‘hugging and learning’. I myself think Seinfeld is about as funny as watching a family pet get hit by a car, but they made a good point about the way sitcoms have to reset between episodes. If characters grow and learn too much, they will no longer be foolish enough to get into the situations where they can be funny. For the sitcom to be funny, Basil Fawlty cannot learn to stop being a fawning snob; Father Ted Crilly can never priest up and take his job seriously; Ross in Friends can never quite lose the stick up his butt. Seinfeld itself deferred its characters from learning anything for so long that the only way they could finally end the show was to send the characters to prison. Both versions of The Office, however, featured personal growth in their characters. In the UK version, Dawn learned the self-confidence to dump Lee and find Tim. Gareth became a semi-decent manager. And David Brent met a woman who liked him, and finally acquired the balls to tell Chris Finch to fuck off—my favourite moment in the UK version. Perhaps only Tim didn’t grow, but only because he started out relatively mature. The US version, however, took the idea of ‘growth’ and hugely expanded and elaborated on it. Which made it more ambitious and, I think, ultimately more impressive than the UK version. Which brings me to my theory. My theory about the US version of The Office is that it works, on one level, as a spiritual epic about the development of personhood from infancy to maturity. Now, I’m sure that this will hardly come as a surprise. Obviously, Michael Scott develops enormously from his beginning in season 1 to his end in season 7. He begins as an utterly self-absorbed manchild, with poor relationships with other people and a weak but malicious sense of humour, which switches itself off whenever he feels like people are laughing at him, rather than at his crappy jokes. However, by the end, he is in a happy and secure marriage with someone who loves him, and indeed they have children, of whom he is so proud that he owns two phones, just to hold all the pictures of them. (This was before cloud storage really took off.) But, you see, my theory is that The Office is not primarily about the development of Michael’s soul. It’s also about the development of Dwight’s. Obviously, Michael is the biggest manchild in the office: the character who most desperately needs to grow up. But Dwight, at least in the first two seasons, is his loyal lieutenant. What does it say about you when you’re so loyal to such an idiot? I think it says that you have so much more to unlearn. For much of the show, Michael oscillates between childish self-absorption and selfishness, and an almost palpable and rather endearing adoration of, or at least startling empathy for, his employees. But, while Michael in season 2’s ‘Christmas Party’ is mostly a whiny, selfish idiot, in the following episode, ‘Booze Cruise’, he yaws between his worst and his best. He takes the staff on a booze cruise, where Jim is crushed that Pam’s fiancé Roy finally sets a date for their wedding. Jim admits to Michael that he’s dejected about this, but Michael, who himself has been humiliated over the captain of their vessel putting him in his place, is surprisingly encouraging: Michael: Yep. Well, Pam is cute. Jim: Yeah. She's really funny, and she's warm. And she's just... well, anyway. Michael: Well, if you like her so much, don't give up. Jim: She's engaged. Michael: BFD. Engaged ain't married. Jim: Huh. Michael: Never, ever, ever give up. In the episode ‘Email Surveillance’, Michael muses on his relationship with his staff: There's always a distance between a boss and the employees. It is just nature's rule. It's intimidation mostly, it's the awareness that they are not me. I do think that I am very approachable, as one of the guys. But the whole point of that episode is that Michael spends it completely failing to realise that his employees are not him. He can’t perceive boundaries. Michael Scott in season 1 craves something or other, but we’re not sure what. By season 2, his character comes into more focus, and we can see that what he really wants is, like all children, to be loved. But the story as a whole puts Michael in the position of a father to the family of his employees. Which is a role Michael has to grow into, because he is comically unfit for it. He wants all the power and love that a benevolent father might get, but for the longest time he can’t give it back, because he’s obsessed with his need to be given it first. However, not all of his employees realise this: only the relatively grown-up ones, such as Jim and Pam. Dwight does not realise it. So, as long as Michael doesn’t grow up, Dwight can’t. In an early episode, Dwight, who as usual is trying to make some wrongheaded point according to his arcane private code, asks Ryan what Michael’s greatest fear is. ‘Loneliness,’ Ryan astutely replies. ‘Maybe women.’ ‘Wrong,’ says Dwight, his eyes gleaming with triumph. ‘Michael Scott isn’t afraid of anything. Also, I would have accepted “snakes”.’ Dwight will pay, elsewhere, for not understanding his ‘father’ better. The responsible children: Jim and Pam Jim and Pam are uneasy in that they know, on some level, that they are mere subordinate players in the drama of Michael’s personal development, and are eager for him to grow up so that they can get the hell out of there. Both of them know Michael’s habits extraordinarily well, because he’s as predictable as an infant. If he eats a family-sized chicken pot pie for lunch, he will fall asleep. If he eats a lot of sugar, he will have a manic sugar rush and then, sure enough, fall asleep. Stanley and Phyllis are the uncle and aunt, although Stanley in particular is uneasy in that role because he wants nothing to do with Michael’s development. In Michael’s mind, Stanley is a sassy, street-smart black mentor to him, not the grumpy white-collar worker that Stanley actually is. Michael treats Phyllis as if she is the office’s resident elderly woman, although, as Phyllis points out, they were in high school together. Whenever Phyllis behaves like an ordinary middle-aged woman with ordinary needs, Michael is squicked out. (There’s one moment early on where she does an expert dancer’s shimmy, and Michael practically runs out of the room; in her youth, Phyllis Smith was a burlesque performer.) Remember Phyllis’ wedding, where Michael behaved as though he were simultaneously her father and her son? Running around wanting attention, yet also presuming to take charge of proceedings? Dwight is the other-son, the disappointment to Michael, the one who actually gives Michael the loyalty and love Michael craves but which Michael in this instance doesn’t want, because it comes from Dwight. Michael is aware that Dwight is himself highly immature, as witnessed by Dwight’s extreme gullibility and his susceptibility to Jim’s pranks. Jim represents something Michael needs: Dwight, in the early seasons, represents something Michael wants to avoid. If Jim is the golden boy, Dwight is the Tin Man. He thinks he’s on a quest, which is to do awesome things in life, like be a karate expert, or a supervillain: actually, he just needs to grow a heart. Dwight’s estrangement from the world of society has something to do how he seems to belong to a different century. In season 5 ep 5, ‘Crime Aid’, he mentions that Angela has ‘introduced’ him to, among other things, pasteurised milk, sheets and monotheism. It’s as if the Schrutes are some weird, inbred, Lovecraftian clan, and Dwight has a mutant brother who dwells beneath the beets. Dwight’s immaturity rears its head in season 3’s ‘The Coup’, where he mistakes the story he is in for a political thriller, instead of a family drama. Angela encourages him to take over the office from Michael, so Dwight arranges a meeting in a diner with Jan where he lays out his idea that she should make him manager. I thought it was interesting that, in this meeting, Dwight is stuffing his face with waffles and sausage, whereas Jan confines herself to sipping coffee. This subtly emphasises how needy and appetite-driven Dwight is, and how cool and collected Jan is (at this point in the show, anyway.) Dwight mistakes himself for someone with the same status as Michael. He expects Jan to calculate that he would be a suitable replacement and behave accordingly. Jan, who knows that she is not in a political thriller, interprets Dwight’s demand not as a power move but as ordinary insubordination, and bluntly instructs Michael to get his office in order. And here’s where the family dynamic plays out. Michael treats Dwight’s professional betrayal of him as something intensely personal and familial. Dwight’s excuse for leaving the office to meet Jan was that he was at the dentist, so Michael, simmering with barely concealed rage, asks him the dentist’s name: Dwight, who is terrible at deception, can only come up with ‘Crentist’. Michael proceeds to closely inspect Dwight’s teeth (this scene is so weird) and eventually confronts him with the knowledge that he knows everything. A humbled Dwight grovels pathetically on the floor, sobbing. The emotion in this scene goes way beyond anything necessary for a boss reprimanding an employee. But a) it’s funny to see Dwight’s hubris go boing and rebound in his face, and b) it underlines Michael’s quasi-paternal relationship to Dwight. It’s an Oedipal situation, except Oedipus doesn’t kill Laius: he just unsuccessfully tries to take over the office from him. (Michael may also be unconsciously disturbed that Dwight went behind his back to Jan, who Michael regards—not very accurately—as a former lover.) When, in season 4’s ‘Did I Stutter?’, Stanley is publicly insubordinate to Michael in a less serious way, Michael is able to recognise that Stanley is not part of his line of succession, and is able to take Stanley aside, admit that he knows Stanley doesn’t respect him, and tell him that, nevertheless, Stanley can’t talk to him like that. Stanley, perhaps relieved to be recognised for once as who he is, agrees to be less snarky in future. Michael grows up, a little. The film crew is the mirror in which Michael sees himself as the man he would like to be. The film crew’s presence encourages Michael to perform, all the time: perform the role of world’s best boss, father to his people, office joker, cool guy, politically incorrect rebel, sensitive advocate for diversity—whatever his little mind feels like doing on any given day. We need to talk about Todd Packer. Packer is Michael’s evil twin, another irresponsible and self-centred manchild, except that Packer entirely lacks Michael’s need to be loved. Packer is solely interested in following his every last immediate impulse. It’s not that he’s anti-social: that would imply an intellectual attitude, which Packer is not capable of having. It’s that society means nothing to him. Again, not unlike an infant. Packer’s resemblance to an infant, and the threat he represents to Michael ever achieving maturity, is first shown in season 2’s ‘The Carpet’, where Michael discovers that something foul-smelling (it’s implied to be human faeces) has been left on his office carpet. He is disgusted by this and is plunged into depression as to who in the office would do something so horrible to him—until Packer gleefully informs him that he, Packer, did it, whereupon Michael declares it hilarious. Watching the scene where Michael realises it was Packer, I can never quite decide whether his prolonged laughter and applause is meant to seem rather forced—like he knows he ought to find it funny and is doing his best to perform amusement for Packer—or whether he is genuinely very relieved to learn that it was just Packer being Packer, and not someone who secretly dislikes him. A tribute to Steve Carell’s acting. Throughout the episode, Michael behaves like a mini-Packer, randomly thumping Creed on the arm and then getting Dwight to join him in a ‘raid’ on the accounting department. It’s Michael living up to the idea of cool that Packer represents to him, even though it amounts to no more than random assholism. Still, ‘The Carpet’ is the last time Michael wholeheartedly endorses Packer. When Packer took a dump on Michael’s carpet, he finally did the thing that made Michael begin to think of Packer as someone who had to be excused. And here we need to go back to Jan Levinson. I would insert a picture of Melora Hardin as Jan, here, but one of the interesting things about Jan, which makes her unlike Jim, or David Wallace, or Todd Packer, is that no one picture can be said to show what Jan looks like. This is because Jan’s role changes so much. In the first season and a half, Jan is basically the all-father, the ultimate authority figure, the person with the power to order Michael what to do, and reprimand him for doing things badly. Jan is the line beyond which no-one may cross. However, because The Office is a comedy and not an academic paper, this is disrupted from the very start by Michael finding her attractive. The tension between Jan’s unquestionable authority and her presence as a person gets stretched and snapped in the crucial season 2 episode ‘The Client’, where for the first time we see Michael Scott operating in the sphere of his competence. I’m sure you know the story, and skip the next bit if you do. ‘The Client’: skippable synopsis Jan has arranged for her and Michael to meet a client at the Radisson hotel for lunch, to broker a deal where Dunder Mifflin will supply paper to local government. The client, Christian, has to cut costs, and Dunder Mifflin are more expensive than their big chain competitors. Michael switches the meeting to his favourite local restaurant, Chili’s, without Jan’s permission. When they meet the client, Jan tries to talk business but Michael insists on making small talk and ordering food and drinks. What was supposed to be a lunch meeting goes on until late in the evening, and by the end of it, Christian has come to like Michael so much that he’s persuaded by Michael that Dunder Mifflin’s customer service justifies the extra cost. Jan is so impressed that she kisses Michael in the parking lot. This is only the beginning of Jan’s character development. Dunderpedia notes that her original name, Jan Levinson-Gould, seems to have the surnames of two of the psychologists most associated with the concept of the midlife crisis, Daniel Levinson and Roger Gould, although they add ‘this is probably just a coincidence’. I think not: Jan is, as they also say, ‘the epitome of a midlife crisis’. Jan’s turn from no-nonsense authority figure, to girlfriend from hell, to hospital administrator and single mother who’s recorded an entire album of cover versions of songs made famous by Doris Day, is one of the great joys of the show, thanks in part to Melora Hardin’s wilingness to play Jan as a complete nutjob. Jan’s most sympathetic moment and her least come very close to each other, in season 4, after she’s been fired from Dunder Mifflin for screwing up at work too often. By season 4 episodes 7/8, ‘Money’, she has moved into Michael’s condo. Michael, now the sole earner in their relationship, quickly runs into money problems, which he attempts to solve by declaring bankruptcy, except that he’s under the impression that you do that by walking into a public place and saying in a loud voice, ‘I… DECLARE… BANK-RUPT-CYYYYYY!’ Michael attempts to get rid of his money problems by literally climbing onto a freight train, but Jan comes to find him, and tells him that he is the one person who has stuck by her in difficult times, and they walk off holding hands. However, three episodes later, in ‘Survivor Man’, Michael becomes annoyed that Ryan did not invite him on a survival weekend. Convinced that he needs to undergo a wilderness ordeal, he decides to go on one by himself, getting Dwight to take him deep into the forest and leaving him there with only a knife and a roll of duct tape. Unknown to him, Dwight remains behind to keep an eye on him, using the scope on his hunting rifle as a telescope. (Dwight’s own paternal instincts finally kicking in.) Of course, Michael utterly fails to find food and shelter, succeeding only in destroying his suit, and only when he ingests some random mushrooms does Dwight come charging out of hiding and force him to spit them out (in a peculiar reversal of Michael’s inspection of Dwight’s teeth in ‘The Coup’). Cured of the need to prove himself in the wild, Michael returns to the office, where his newfound enthusiasm for the office and its comforts bucks him up, and he single-handedly rescues Jim’s lame attempt to organise a combined birthday. This plays directly into the next episode, ‘The Deposition’, in which Michael has to testify in Jan’s wrongful dismissal suit against the company. During the deposition, Michael realises that Jan has submitted his personal diary as evidence, with neither his knowledge nor permission. He further realises that she gave him a bad performance review after they had started dating. Finally, he learns that he was never seriously considered for a corporate position. Nevertheless, he defends the company against Jan, earning the gratitude of David Wallace, the CFO. Michael’s verdict is ‘You expect to get screwed by your company, but you never expect to get screwed by your girlfriend.’ The angry silence in which Michael and Jan drive home is the smouldering mound of garbage that ignites in the next episode, one of the show’s very greatest: ‘Dinner Party’. Jan in ‘Dinner Party’, becoming the devil. ‘Dinner Party’ is one of the ultimate examples of the family dynamic in the show, with Michael and Jan as warring parents, and Jim, Pam, Andy and Angela as their more or less mortified children witnessing the break-up. Andy, true to form, is so self-absorbed that he’s largely oblivious to the intensely radioactive cloud of passive-aggression that’s boiling between Michael and Jan, while Jim and Pam start out by finding it funny, and end up finding it excruciating. One touch which I cite in support of my theory: when the guests have already been there for some time, Pam is distressed to find out that Jan hasn’t even started cooking the osso buco yet. Jan will later shower love on her own daughter, but at this stage she can’t provide for her symbolic ‘children’, Jim, Pam, Andy and Angela. In ‘Dinner Party’ we learn that Jan has taken over an entire room of Michael’s condo for her experiments in candle-making, and forces Michael to sleep on a tiny bench at the foot of his own bed. (In, we may note for psychoanalytical reasons, the fetal position.) ‘Dinner Party’ is, among other things, a masterclass in tight-lipped smiling. It’s also, I would argue, the American show’s ultimate revenge on the British show, in terms of cringe comedy. The whole episode piles awkwardness upon hideous awkwardness, climaxing with Michael’s lament about the physical toll that multiple vasectomies have taken on his body. For once, the chief source of awkwardness is not Dwight, who crashes the party with his date, his former babysitter, and who seems relatively sane, compared to Michael with his comically tiny plasma screen television, and Jan compulsively dancing and crooning along to her former assistant Hunter’s awful CD. Dwight has also come prepared, bringing his own food in the form of turkey legs and beet salad, thereby underlining that he can survive in this god-awful house but Jim and Pam must go hungry. (In a nice touch, Jim steals Hunter’s CD, as a sort of punishment for the surrogate parents’ dreadful dinner party, and he and Pam enjoy it while contentedly munching burgers in their car, later that evening.) The entire stretch from ‘Money’ to ‘Dinner Party’ is the trauma that fatally cracks the Michael/Jan axis. In the immediate aftermath of it, Dwight rescues Michael from Jan. Michael regresses so far beyond helplessness that, when he’s riding in Dwight’s car to spend the night at Dwight’s house, he sticks his head out of the window like a dog. But although Jan does return, she is never again the force of nature that she is here. She is not, in the end, the paternal authority figure that Michael still needs to measure himself by. That figure is David Wallace. Who I’ve discussed separately. Which brings us, at long last, to Holly Flax. Holly is, quite possibly, the nicest person in the show. She was created to be possibly Michael’s love interest. Amy Ryan said on the Office Ladies podcast that she was initially booked for only one episode, and she understood that whether or not Holly would actually become his love interest depended in large part on how well she did in the role. She was meant to be the first character who simply liked Michael: an amiable, rather dorky woman who used bad jokes and funny voices and mild sarcasm as a way of negotiating awkwardness. In terms of the family dynamic that I describe in this show, it makes perfect sense that Holly is Toby’s replacement in HR. Michael hates HR. Or rather, he thinks he hates HR. Actually he just hates Toby. I think that the reason Michael loathes Toby so much is not just Toby’s low-key, mumbly, lukewarm personality (and let’s hear it for Paul Lieberstein’s self-effacing performance) but because Toby, as HR person, represents the accumulated wisdom of the universe about all the lessons Michael desperately needs to learn in life, but, because he’s Toby, Michael can’t bear to learn those lessons from him. Michael can’t stand to be schooled by someone so entirely unlike him: such a droopy, dreary, brown-suited killjoy. So, when Holly shows up in season 4’s ‘Goodbye Toby’, Michael is initially suspicious, but when he finally meets her, she succeeds in completely disarming him by distinguishing herself from Toby, in front of Toby: Michael: Hi. Yeah. Right. Okay, well, they hired a female Toby. Good for the world. Thank you, God, for creating two of you. Here's how things work here: my job is to make the office fun. Your job is to make the office lame. And we have an eternal struggle, you and I. And only one of us can be the winner. Spoiler alert: I'm gonna win. Holly: Man, someone doesn't like HR. Michael: Yeah. Holly: [to Toby] What did you do to him? Toby: Nothing. Michael: No. He tortured me... with his awfulness. Holly: [smiling] Yeah, I know what you mean. I nearly fell asleep when he gave me a tour of the files. Holly manages to say this without unduly offending Toby, almost as if she’s gently mocking Michael for having such a ridiculously low opinion of Toby. But it serves to flip Michael completely in her favour. Because, as everyone who’s watched this show knows, Holly is in many ways a female version of Michael. In fact, I’ll go further: she is, in terms of the spiritual epic that I maintain lies beneath this whole show, the missing half of Michael. Besides having similar verbal habits, such as doing impressions of people and then murmuring the name of the person she’s just done an impression of, she gets Michael, recognising all of his good qualities and noticing (at least at first) none of his bad ones. Holly brings human resources to Michael. Ryan’s acting convinces us that Holly is a genuinely warm person, such as the way she interacts with Kevin, who she has been told by Dwight is mentally handicapped. Because Kevin is Kevin, this is not all that hard to believe (even though Kevin is quite capable of displaying remarkable savvy when he wants to.) Of course, Holly’s beaming smile and general kindness only convinces Kevin that she’s super into him. Michael’s growth accelerates dramatically as soon as he’s met her. In season 5 episode 3’s ‘Business Ethics’, Holly attempts to conduct an ethics seminar in the office, after it’s revealed that Meredith has been sleeping with a supplier in return for discounts. The seminar collapses because the staff aren’t interested, and when Michael attempts to tell Holly that it doesn’t matter, it doesn’t work, because she is genuinely upset at Meredith’s breach of ethics. Then, he is present when Holly’s line manager brusquely chews her out over the phone, telling her to stop trying to do her job properly, and just get the staff to sign the papers saying that they’ve had the seminar, because never mind about the stupid ethics, the company needs the discount. Michael does not joke about this, nor is he triumphant that he’s been proved right. Instead, when he’s alone, he asks the camera one of the wisest questions he’s ever asked: How do you tell someone you care about deeply, ‘I told you so?’ He muses on various different ways of doing this, and being Michael he settles on the obviously wrong way—but then, crucially, he doesn’t do it. He lets it go. By the next episode, all is forgotten and the office likes Holly again. Holly is an element in Michael’s universe that is both subversive and healing. She uses her common sense and sympathy to expel him from the infantile world of fantasy that he lives in, and consoles him with her mere presence for that expulsion. When she is sent back to Nashua, this process is only half complete, and so he is sorely wounded. Remember that Holly was not some late-stage element in the show. She got introduced at the end of season 4, she’s whisked away only a few episodes later in season 5 ep 6 ‘Employee Transfer’, and does not properly return until ‘Classy Christmas’, halfway through season 7. For most of the intervening period, more than two whole seasons of the show, Michael is more or less secretly pining for her. At the end of season 5 ep 7’s ‘Business Trip’, his sudden question to David Wallace is as real and as honest and as authentically sorrowful as Michael ever gets: Michael: No, David, you listen to me. Why did you send her away? That—God. You knew I liked her and you just sent her away. And that… that was a sucky thing to do, man. David Wallace: Michael, sometimes— Michael: That was a really sucky thing to do. David Wallace: Sometimes, we— [Michael hangs up on him.] The childish word ‘sucky’ reminds us of the little boy Michael who we saw in a clip from an old TV show in season 2, telling a puppet that his dream was to get married and have one hundred kids, so I can have one hundred friends, and no one can say ‘no’ to being my friend. That is the yawning abyss of loneliness within Michael. That is what goes away when he’s around Holly. By season 6 ep 6 ‘Whistleblower’, Dunder Mifflin has been taken over by a larger company, Sabre, and David Wallace is out. The new boss, Jo Bennett, is an ambiguous figure with regard to Michael’s development: neither a father- nor a mother-figure. Michael struggles to adapt to her being the new boss, which involves him standing up to her; it doesn’t get the results he wants, but it does make him feel more grown-up. When it turns out that Sabre printers have a tendency to catch fire, Jo knows that the company has to make some sort of recognition of this, but she has very good reasons for not wanting to: Jo: When I was growing up, there was nothing better than being a big old business tycoon. And I thought I'd break that glass ceiling and be a hero to all those little girls out there... and they'd make a Barbie out of me. […] I, did I sell cheap printers? I do. But if I have to go out there in front of the press and make one of them public apology recalls, I mean, it's all I'll ever be remembered for. Nobody will want to play with my Barbie. Michael: You know, I would be willing, under the right circumstances, to do that for you. So Michael does do that, and at the end of the episode, Jo is appreciative: Jo: I hope your rough patch ends soon. Michael: Thanks. Today helped. Jo: Well, give me a shout if I can brighten your life. Michael: Okay. Hey, [jokingly] you could transfer Holly back from Nashua. Jo: Let me see what I can do. Michael looks… stunned. The very next episode of the show has, as its cold open, the lip dub, where almost the entire office dances and lip-syncs to the Human Beinz’ ‘Nobody But Me’. It’s there because that’s the only possible reaction the show can have to the idea that Holly may return. A goofy explosion of joy and good humour. Even Dwight gets in on it, although being Dwight he goes too far. Only Darryl and Angela remain on the outside, Angela because I said I didn’t want to be on the internet! and Darryl so that Angela can have someone to shut herself in a side office with. I think the ultimate example of Holly directly influencing Michael’s growth comes in season 7’s ‘Threat Level Midnight’. This is the completion of a stage that began in season 5 ep 11/12, ‘Stress Relief’, where Michael organised a roast of himself, and then found that he couldn’t handle people laughing at him. After going to the park and being by himself for a while, he comes back and quick-fire insults the entire staff, and an increasingly tense moment is defused when he tells Stanley You crush your wife during sex and your heart sucks, and Stanley finds this hilarious. Having got even with his ‘children’, Michael visibly relaxes, tells them he’s kidding, and sincerely adds, You guys are the reason I went into the paper business. He has at last learned the grade-school-level lesson of being able to take a joke. Two seasons later, in ‘Threat Level Midnight’, Michael has finally finished the terrible movie he’s been making for years, using the office staff as cast. He announces that he’ll screen it for everyone. Pam prepares them for it by reminding them that the last time he screened an unfinished version of it, they all laughed and he got mortally offended. She urges them not to laugh this time, and for most of the first half of the screening, the staff manage to keep a respectful silence. However, Pam herself shatters the strenuous politeness when she exclaims in horror at seeing her mom playing a sexy nurse, and then Jim can’t keep it in anymore when he sees the absurd dance sequence, ‘The Scarn’. Michael has a hissy fit and stops the screening. Outside the conference room, he goes to Holly for confirmation that his masterpiece isn’t just laughable nonsense, but she can’t give it to him. Look at the sheer economy of how B.J. Novak wrote this conversation: Michael: No, no. Holly, this isn't Ocean's Eleven, where you get together with all your friends and just have fun and don't care about how it turns out. What'd you really think, honestly. Holly: Um... Michael: Is it, is it because you're afraid of where this is gonna take me? See, because I need you... to keep me grounded. Holly: [deadpan] Not worried about that. (Holly’s sarcasm is nicely understated.) Michael: [angrily] It was eleven years, okay? This has been my dream for eleven years, and if you don't think it's great than you're basically saying that you don't believe in my dream. Holly: Wha- It's your dream and you never even mentioned it before! Michael is still clinging to the illusion that ‘Threat Level Midnight’ has a future outside of this office, and that it’s more than something where you get together with all your friends and just have fun and don’t care about how it turns out. Still, there’s an element of realism to his awareness that, if a manager of a paper office in Scranton, PA is going to make a film which he wants people to take seriously, it had better be more than just an Ocean’s Eleven-type of film. (And I’m thinking more the slack and self-indulgent 1960 Ocean’s 11, than the slick 2001 Ocean’s Eleven.) Michael: I talk about a lot of things, Holly! I was eventually gonna get around to my dream! Obviously! Eleven years I could've been working on the Scarn Nebulus. Holly: Well, why do you have to make a movie at all? Michael: Because, if I don't have this, what do I have? I have nothing. Holly: Really, you can't think of anything else that you might have? The armour-piercing question. Michael: I have my book on business, Somehow I Manage. I have my HBO comedy special, Here I Go Again… But you know what? When I think about it, when I really think about it, none of those things are as real to me as my movie. Holly: I'm real. Michael: Yeah, you're a real pain in the ass. And I'm gonna go watch the movie with people who think it's great! And I'm sorry I called you a pain in the ass, I'm angry, and I love you. Holly: I love you too. He couldn’t stand the idea that people were laughing at what it is, as opposed to what he wanted it to be. But she has got to him. Because, before, he would never have sincerely apologised to someone he was in the middle of a fight with. And he would never have been able to accurately assess his own motivations, and he would never have been able to remember, while still angry, that he loved that person. He and Jan do have a superficially similar I love you/I love you moment at the end of ‘The Deposition’ but in context, it’s cold and unconvincing. Here, it’s two lovers reassuring each other that their love is stronger than this fight, but yes, they’re still definitely having a fight. He asks the staff if they want to watch the rest of it. They say that they do. He puts it on again. And this time around, Michael is no longer in his bubble of comforting illusions. Holly is in the next room, more real to him than his movie is. He’s no longer seeing the movie that he wanted it to be: he’s seeing it through the eyes of everyone else in the room. That’s why he’s no longer watching in a tense silence. He’s remembering the shoot and how much fun it was. He starts laughing. Because it’s hilariously bad, and he can see that now. He gets up and goes out to her. Holly: Hey, I'm sorry. It is good. Michael: No it's not. [smiles, kisses her] It's not. But, they really seem to be enjoying it. It doesn’t matter that it’s terrible. That’s actually what’s good about it. This moment seems to me to be a version of one of those archetypal moments in stories—not necessarily American stories—where a character realises who they are, and humbly or bravely accepts a humdrum reality as opposed to a grandiose fantasy. I’d compare it to the great moment towards the end of Toy Story, when Woody brings it home to a dejected Buzz that he is not a Space Ranger, but a beloved children’s toy. Buzz becomes more himself, and finally learns his true value. It is one of the pivotal moments for Michael: a moment when he realises, and accepts, his true stature in his life. The next thing that has to happen is that he has to psychologically detach himself from Packer. It happens in the very next episode, which is named after Packer. Packer is back in the office, and spends the episode being his usual obnoxious self, and both Jim and Dwight loathe him, but Michael laughs dutifully as always, and is keen for Holly to like him. But after Holly’s observed Packer at length, she refuses to take the bait, and bluntly describes Packer as a ‘jerk’. Michael is confused, and tries to cling onto the image of Packer as a fun-loving master of misrule. When Jim and Dwight team up to prank Packer into going to Florida, pretending to him that he’s been offered a job there, Michael is outraged, and tells them he will tell Packer. But Packer tells Michael, I'm gonna tell you something that none of these people have the stones to tell you. It's your girlfriend, man. She's uptight. Michael freezes. Packer has insulted the person closest to his heart. He doesn’t tell Packer about the prank. Packer goes to Florida. Four episodes later, Michael leaves Dunder Mifflin, and the show, to live in Colorado with Holly. It’s symbolically interesting that Michael’s departure is so low-key and so understated. The attention-needing Michael of seasons 1–3 couldn’t possibly have left the show. But in ‘Goodbye Michael’, he leaves the office a day earlier than he told everyone he would, because all he wants is to be with Holly and he doesn’t want big goodbyes. Only Jim figures it out, and he and Michael say an emotional goodbye by discussing the goodbyes that they will never make, at the lunch they plan to have ‘tomorrow’, that they know they will never have. Michael’s departure is rather like the unexpected death of a family member: one minute they’re there and you’re making plans, then they’re gone. At the airport, a visibly more cheerful Michael takes off his radio mic, bids the film crew goodbye with a last That’s what she said gag, and casually ambles off, independent, free at last from the need to perform for the camera. He is intercepted by Pam, and they share a silent goodbye (this shot was Jenna Fischer and Steve Carell actually saying goodbye, on Carell’s last day.) Once Michael has left the show, and the symbolic death-of-the-father has happened, the remaining characters are free to grow up as they will. The symbolic death of Packer is part of this. He returns for the season 8 Florida sequences. In ‘Last Day in Florida’, a quiet hint from Robert California warns Jim that, if Dwight claims credit for the Sabre store, he will get fired because Robert was never interested in the store. Jim physically tackles Dwight to the ground, warning him not to make the presentation, and stalls Dwight for long enough that Nellie has Packer do it—whereupon Packer gets canned, which Dwight sees. A chastened Dwight silently extends his hand to Jim and helps him up off the floor. Jim and Dwight have become true brothers. Never again do they resume their former antagonism. In the last season of the show, Jim and Pam negotiate marital troubles, and Dwight finally, ruefully accepts that he has screwed up too many times to become manager. The latter is a crucial moment for him. He has stopped living his life like he is a broadsword-wielding knight errant, or (as on his bad days) like he’s a Bond villain. At long last, he behaves like a salesman in a paper company, the job he excels at. He even says that Jim should be manager instead of him. Jim, for his part, is content to be an underachieving paper salesman with a loving family, and has abandoned his plans to switch jobs to the now-thriving business he helped found. There’s just one thing he didn’t reckon on. Pam doesn’t find the office any more magical than Jim does, and she is upset to think that this, after all, is who they are, when she knows that they could do better. In the last moments of the show, she pulls the second-bravest stunt of her life: she sells their house, so that they can move to Austin and Jim can have his ideal job. But in the meantime, Jim becomes Dwight’s best man, and Dwight refers to Pam as his ‘best friend’. And it’s true that Dwight is one of the few male characters in the show who never professes any romantic or sexual interest in Pam—which makes sense if you think of them as, symbolically, brother and sister. (He does once talk with characteristically brutal frankness about how she’s not as attractive as she was before she had children, but he never seems to be attracted to her.) Still and all, when Jim has loyally discharged his Bestischmensch duties, he does the only thing he can possible do, which is step aside and bring back, from the symbolic dead, the spiritual father, Michael, to be the true Bestischmensch for Dwight. I think it’s significant that, in the Finale, Michael—who, for the first time, barely even acknowledges the camera—has only two lines: Dwight: [turns around] [amazed] Michael. I can't believe you came. Michael: That's what she said. And: Michael: [crying] I feel like all my kids grew up and then they married each other… It's every parent's dream. I rest my case. There are a lot of things I’ve left out of what’s already a very long answer. I didn’t talk about all the episodes which also support this theory—and also all the ones that undermine it. I didn’t talk about the show’s more dodgy episodes, such as season 3’s ‘A Benihana Christmas’, where one joke turns on Michael’s inability to tell his date from another woman (because they’re both Benihana waitresses, and all Asian people look alike, you see.)
