I didn’t talk about capitalism. And I could have. But I didn’t. Be grateful you were spared that. If my very long exposition of this theory has entertained you, that’s all it was meant to do. Do I really, honestly believe it? Sure, let’s go with that. I think, however, that this theory helps to explain why some people, like me, consider the US version of the show to be be superior to the UK version. I’ve heard the US version dismissed as a ‘soap opera’, or as somehow lacking the edge of the UK version. I disagree; the UK version never got anything like as intimately nasty as ‘Dinner Party’. I think the US version is a much more ambitious and much more successful piece of entertainment. It’s longer, and tougher, and has more twists and turns, and it’s more fleshed-out, but when you take the whole thing as it comes, it’s a great deal more satisfying. … That’s what she said. Not so much sources as books and websites that helped inform how I thought about this answer: The Wikipedia and TV Tropes pages were very helpful, as was the very thorough The Office wiki, Dunderpedia (Dunderpedia: The Office Wiki), especially for keeping track of which characters appear in which episodes. Jenna Fischer and Angela Kinsey’s wonderful Office Ladies podcast was also very useful. Roland Barthes, Critical Essays, trans. Norton, 2006 Thanks for reading.

Question: What exactly is studied in musicology, and how does it differ from music history?
Answer: Music history is simply the history of music—although nothing is simple, and how we tell the history depends a lot on our assumptions about how history works. Older styles of music history tend to tell it as a history of great composers, but more modern approaches (for example, the volumes in the Cambridge History series) take a more thematic or genre-based approach. It’s difficult to say ‘exactly’ what is studied in musicology, because the nature of the subject itself changes over time, and so do definitions of it. The late Joe Kerman was one of the 20th century’s greatest musicologists, and someone whose work I have the greatest admiration for. Joseph Kerman, 1924–2014 Kerman noted in his 1985 book Musicology that: the word was originally understood (as Musikwissenschaft still is) to cover thinking about, research into, and knowledge of all possible aspects of music. However, Kerman added: But in academic practice, and in broad general usage, musicology has come to have a much more constricted meaning. It has come to mean the study of the history of Western music in the high-art tradition. […] Musicology is perceived as dealing essentially with the factual, the documentary, the verifiable, the analysable, the positivistic. Musicologists are respected for the facts they know about music. They are not admired for their insight into music as aesthetic experience. He went on to say: Which is the subject of this book—musicology in the ideal, comprehensive, original definition, or musicology in the restricted, more mundane, current one? The broad or the narrow? The answer lies somewhere in between. Kerman goes on to discuss the overlaps between musicology, theory and ethnomusicology—all of which disciplines were a bit more separate from each other forty years ago, when he wrote the book, than they are now. I would say that one effect of the revolution in musicology brought about by Kerman and younger colleagues of his, such as Philip Brett, Susan McClary and Lawrence Kramer, is that the original, broader definition of musicology has become much more accepted in practice than the narrower one. The influence of the narrower one still lingers, especially in the tendency many people have to place ‘Western music in the high-art tradition’ at the top of a sort of pyramid of ‘musical quality’. But the new musicology, which got going in the 1980s, is much more willing to pay attention to other forms of music and take them seriously, and is also more ready to talk about the aesthetic experience of music, than the kind that focused on musical analyses of works of Western classical music, as if no other kind of music deserved such close attention. (I would add a link to the Wikipedia article on the new musicology, but as is the way with so many Wikipedia articles about subjects one actually knows a little bit about, I can’t honestly recommend it.) (I would separate the musicology of popular music from a cultural studies approach to popular music. The former tends to pay more close attention to the music itself, the latter to its context and its relationship to the culture. I’m currently reading a book-length study of the music of Kate Bush, Ron Moy’s Kate Bush and Hounds of Love, which is written from a cultural studies perspective rather than a musicological one, and which suffers accordingly, IMO. Hopefully the next book on my reading list, Dan Charnas’ Dilla Time, about the life, music and cultural afterlife of Detroit hip-hop producer J Dilla, will delve a bit deeper into Dilla’s music than Moy does into Bush’s. Edit: It does. It’s shaping up to be one of the most remarkable books about popular music I’ve ever read.) So, musicology is not solely concerned with music history, or musical analysis, but it can encompass those things while taking a broader look at music in general, and trying to promote an understanding of it.

Question: I play cello. Would it be easier for me to learn the bass guitar since I can read bass clef and I have the strength and stamina to pluck?
Answer: Very good question. It so happens that I have had cellist friends, and I play the bass guitar. Well, sometimes. First question: easier than what? You don’t specify. Bass guitar does require some core strength—you got to strap that baby on and move your fretting hand around quite a bit, and I find that my plucking hand also gets quite a workout. I would say that, for the sake of timbral variation, and if you’re playing a bass that has more than one pickup, a good player needs to be able to pluck with equal power and precision in at least three places: nearer the neck; between the neck and the bridge; and nearer the bridge. And plucking near the bridge is hard, because the strings are harder to get going there. Other answerers have observed that the cello is tuned in fifths, CGDA, whereas the bass guitar is tuned like the double bass, EADG. This is something that you’ll have to get used to. Except: Wait, Alex—is there by any chance a precedent for a cellist taking up the bass guitar and tuning it like a cello? Why, yes there is! That rather grainy photo is of Georgina Born, an English cellist who joined the radical prog-rock band Henry Cow in 1976. She joined as their bass player, and tuned her bass guitar down to cello tuning. If you want to know about Henry Cow, I wrote about them here: Here she is rather more visibly, with her Ampeg bass: Anyway, Georgina Born tuned her bass like a cello, and played some great basslines with it. However, it might be easier in the long run to tune the bass normally. In any case, I see no reason why you shouldn’t take to the bass with ease. And if you want something to practice bass with which you may be familiar, I have this book and I recommend it: Enjoy!

Question: Do any restaurants serve food named after famous people? Has anyone ever had something named after them by their favorite place to eat?
Answer: The Savoy Grill in London still serves a variant on Omelette Arnold Bennett. Arnold Bennett (1867–1931) was an English writer whose excellent Wikipedia article happens to be today’s featured article. I’ve never actually read him, partly because one of his biggest fans, the English academic John Carey, is in my opinion one of the most cloth-brained chowderheads to rise to a major Oxbridge professorship. But Arnold Bennett liked to dine at the Savoy (he made a ton of money from writing, and was commendably generous with it), and the head chef once made him a bespoke omelette with smoked haddock and a cheese sauce. Bennett liked it so much that he used to ask it to be made for him, and it ended up being named after him. I’ve made it for myself. It’s not hard to make, astonishingly rich and surprisingly cheap, but you don’t want to do anything afterwards except go to bed. And not engage in strenuous exercise. Anyway, the Savoy will do you a Soufflé Arnold Bennett, which is a bit classier.

Question: Are podcasts actually, for the most part, polished mansplaining?
Answer: No, podcasts are not any sort of mansplaining. The defining characteristic of mansplaining is not that it is merely any explanation of anything that is given by a man, but that it is an explanation which is unasked-for and unwanted. Double points if the mansplainer is attempting to explain the matter in hand to an expert on the subject. It just happens that men are vastly more likely to mansplain than women are. I know I am, and so are a lot of men I know, but very few women. Which is why I have no problem with the term, and get impatient with men who attempt to dismiss it on the grounds that it’s sexist, or whatever. (Suck it up, snowflakes: you know we do this and you know we shouldn’t.) If you’re listening to a podcast, presumably you made the decision to do so, unless you’re being subjected to some rather lame form of torture. Therefore, you can’t perceive it as mansplaining, because you wanted to listen to it. This answer is not mansplaining, either, because the OP asked the question and therefore invited the answer.

Question: I've seen movie stunt doubles look exactly like the main actors. Why don't the stunt person do the acting themselves AND do their own stunts? Wouldn't this be cheaper than paying the actor and stunt person?
Answer: I answered an almost identical question before. You haven’t thought this through. Actors are paid what they are paid because their presence in a movie can guarantee an audience, which guarantees box office revenue. People don’t usually know who stunt performers are, so the presence of a stunt performer does not guarantee an audience; also, this means that actors can have different stunt performers doing their stunts because the stunt performer is not required to be recognised by the audience, and indeed shouldn’t be. They should be mistaken for the actor. If the stunt performer is also doing all the acting, they become famous as actors and so their value goes up, and all of a sudden they aren’t cheap anymore. So that’s why stunt performers a.) don’t do all the acting and b.) are cheaper than actors. As long as they’re passing for the actor in the stunt, they don’t bring people to the movie the way actors do. If they became visible as actors they would become more expensive. It would also be a great deal more expensive to insure them.

Question: Can Led Zeppelin be considered a punk band?
Answer: Ah, one of my least favourite structures of a Quora question: Can [something] be considered as [something else that it does not resemble in any way]? I agree with everyone who says that Led Zeppelin were in no way a punk band. The trouble here is that we have no way of knowing what you think constitutes ‘punk’, Jeannie Jimski, but I think it’s a good faith question and you certainly have some interesting ones (I definitely plan to answer Why aren't the Yardbirds more popular?, because it’s right down my alley). Punk isn’t just a musical thing. It’s also a way of being a band, a way of playing music, an attitude towards the music industry. It’s not a simple or pure thing, although it sort of wishes it were: you can be a punk band and be on a major label. I think punk had ‘compromise’ built into itself from the outset, but that’s OK, because it also had ‘resentment’ and ‘aggression’ built into itself, which are two useful things to have when you feel compromised. Ever get the feeling you’ve been cheated? —John Lydon at the Sex Pistols’ original final concert, Winterland Ballroom, San Francisco, 14 January 1978 Led Zeppelin, as observers including our OP know, grew out of the Yardbirds. The band’s prime mover was Jimmy Page, a seasoned session musician, who had tasted fame with the Yardbirds and had a plan to make it very, very big, as long as he could get the right guys. Jimmy Page was not, like most punks, a music business outsider. By the time he was in a position to get Led Zeppelin together, in 1968, he was a showbusiness veteran. He’d first appeared on British television eleven years earlier, as a 13-year-old skiffle musician: Just for context, this was April 1957. John Lennon and Paul McCartney would not have their fateful encounter at Woolton Fete until 6 July, three months later. Page’s early music career was crippled by his chronic ill health. He kept getting glandular fever. By 1963, he had committed himself to the less strenuous lifestyle of a session musician, although he couldn’t read music. He earned his money by being a nimble and imaginative stylist, at a time when British popular music didn’t have a lot of guitarists like that. He played on many classic 60s recordings by British bands. I’ve heard that he played the rhythm guitar on the Kinks’ ‘You Really Got Me’, although Dave Davies played the guitar solo: if so, Page has the more credit, because the riff in ‘You Really Got Me’ is the entire fucking song. His Beatles connection was that he played some guitar on the incidental music for A Hard Day’s Night, so presumably that’s him twanging away on at least some of those tracks, although I have heard that it was the legendary Vic Flick who played the guitar part on the instrumental version of ‘This Boy’ that accompanies Ringo wandering around London (Vic Flick is most famous for his rendition of the James Bond theme in the early Bond movies.) … Aaaanyway, all this is to show that Jimmy Page was a seasoned music-biz insider by the time he put Led Zeppelin together. So… not a punk, then. The recorded evidence shows that Led Zeppelin started out with a lot of musical ideas, but rather fewer lyrical ones. I am hardly the last person to accuse Led Zeppelin of stealing songwriting credit from black musicians. I even wrote an answer about it, which compared Led Zeppelin album labels from different years, showing how their early pressings denied due credit to songwriters but, after the musicians had successfully taken the band to court, later pressings gave the original writers due credit. However, it’s often said that they simply ‘ripped off black music’, and that’s not the case. Led Zeppelin did not simply play Willie Dixon or Howlin’ Wolf songs louder. They radically reshaped the music into something else. It’s just that, while Page was directing the creation of the new music, Plant—who was supposed to be off writing new lyrics—could seldom be bothered to, at least on the first couple of albums, and ended up singing the original lyrics to the blues songs that Page had completely recomposed, which is what landed them in court years later. However, once Plant started taking his songwriting responsibilities more seriously, he began to write the sort of preposterous but effective nonsense that is one of the reasons why we love Led Zeppelin today. ‘Immigrant Song’: We come from the land of the ice and snow From the midnight sun where the hot springs flow The hammer of the gods Will drive our ships to new lands To fight the horde, sing and cry Valhalla, I am coming ‘The Battle of Evermore’: The Queen of Light took her bow And then she turned to go The Prince of Peace embraced the gloom And walked the night alone Oh, dance in the dark of night Sing to the morning light The dark Lord rides in force tonight And time will tell us all Oh, throw down your plow and hoe Rest not to lock your homes Side by side we wait the might Of the darkest of them all ‘Over the Hills and Far Away’: Many have I loved, and many times been bitten Many times I've gazed along the open road Many times I've lied and many times I've listened Many times I've wondered how much there is to know Many dreams come true, and some have silver linings I live for my dream and a pocketful of gold This is… not punk. As Led Zeppelin became bigger, they became ever more remote from their fans. At one point, they were renting their own airliner: As the Seventies wore on, Zeppelin struggled to remain creative. Their last unequivocally decent album, Presence, came out in early 1976, when punk was really getting going: the Ramones’ first album was out within weeks, and the Sex Pistols’ ‘Anarchy in the UK’ was out in November. Unlike The Who’s Pete Townshend, Led Zeppelin had little sympathy with punk. (Townshend himself had little sympathy with Led Zeppelin, liking them personally but detesting their music.) Their last proper album, In Through the Out Door, was a sign of how lost they had become. Coda was a collection of odds-and-sods, including ‘Wearing and Tearing’, the band’s ‘take on’ or ‘response to’ punk. To my ears, ‘Wearing and Tearing’ is just unconvincing. It sounds like Led Zeppelin anxiously trying to show that they’re still hip, but compared to real punk tracks like the Pistols’ magisterial ‘Holidays in the Sun’, or even post-punk like the Clash’s effortlessly swinging ‘Train in Vain’, it’s fussy and fiddly. Led Zeppelin in their prime were never this desperate to prove anything. They just bulldozed ahead. No, Led Zeppelin were not punk. They represented one of the things that punk had no time for.

Question: How do you start formulating answers in high words, or in general using high language?
Answer: Why, Miss, by ceaseless Hours of Application at the Craft of Writing, incessant Study of the Mother Tongue, and the pursuit of Conversation with such Wits and Sages as are willing to associate with my poor Person, quaffing Beverages where convenient. Much has Man learned, many of the Heavenly Ones has he named, said the German poet, since We have been a Conversation. Alas, his Wits broke soon after, from a Surfeit of Hegelianism. But his Spirit lives on, and I believe the Tourist Shops of Tübingen do a brisk Trade in Environmentally Amiable T-Shirts, emblazoned with Images of his Countenance. Rather than trust the Mechanick Artlessness of the Chat-GPT (I believe it was Mr. Beauclerk who wittily claimed the Ackronym to stand for Gullible Person’s Twaddlemaker), I rely on my Brain, my Knowledge (such as it is) of the Language, and the Powers of my Will to speak Truth garb’d in Noble Words. —When, that is, I can be ars’d to. At other times, Miss, I own that I blether. I rely on my Friends to nudge me, when I seem to have forgot the Difference. I am, Miss, your most obedient Servant, Alex. Johnston

Question: As a religious person, if you were lost in a cold place at night and only had a copy of your holy book, would you use it to start a fire?
Answer: I am not a religious person, but I am interested in religion, and in my Unpublished Fantasy Saga (TM) I have a character who is intensely religious and belongs to a religion who treat their holy book with Islam-like reverence. Copies of the book itself are rare and precious, and have many, many pages, and he’s a scholar of just one part of it, because the book is so long and complex and so partially indecipherable that nobody is an authority on all of it. His own study copy is enormous. He’s a rather puny character but at one point, he’s in a tense situation with a female character who’s well-disposed towards him and two other guys who are extremely malevolent (they’ve already been extremely brutal to our unfortunate scholar, from which the woman character extricated him). A fifth character enters, and tries to take charge and defuse the situation, but then one of the bad guys, feeling like his chance of doing mean things is slipping away, lunges towards the female character. So, on impulse, our very tense and keyed-up scholar literally throws his book at the guy. It knocks the villain down and, unluckily for the villain, he lands in such a way that the boot stand by the fireplace pierces his skull and fatally injures him. Things get worse before they get better, but the main consequence for our scholar is that pages of his Book are now covered in blood and bits of brain, and partially charred. Much of his character development from there is his coming to terms with the fact that, nominally a guardian of the holy book, when it came to a crisis he used it as a weapon to defend someone who is not a member of his religion. I wanted to write a character who, from the outside, is gaining something (a broader sense of human worth—people of his religion do tend to regard everyone else as being stupider and more sinful than them) but who experiences it as, among other things, a falling-off from his previously exalted position. He liked feeling as though he was part of a special people, but boring old human empathy made him instinctively try to protect someone who his religion had told him wasn’t worth protecting. … Also I liked taking literally the metaphor ‘threw the book at him’.

Question: If you could have only 3 guitar pedals, what would you choose and why?
Answer: Hmm. I used to believe that, the more pedals you had at your disposal, the better. In this, I was a follower of the late and indisputably great Robert Quine, a guitarist who had an immense collection of obscure fuzzboxes. The rock critic Lester Bangs, who was a friend of Quine, recalled that Quine used to ring him up and say You have to hear this new box I’ve got, it makes the most offensive noise… Quine was a wonderful player, who made indispensable contributions to recordings by Richard Hell and the Voidoids, Lou Reed, John Zorn and Matthew Sweet. But his love of obscure fuzzboxes, while it worked for him, is not necessarily practical for lesser mortals. For one thing, it’s not very practical to own loads of different pedals and cart them about, on the off-chance that one of them might come in useful. And also, over time, I’ve just come to prefer using fewer pedals. In any case, over nearly 40 years playing, I’ve amassed a small collection. At the moment, I have (in roughly chronological order of acquisition): If you break these down into categories, there are really only five types of pedal here: The Zoom does all of these things and more, but at the price of sucking out your tone. So, while it’s useful if you don’t care that you sound completely digitalised, and sometimes I’m fine with that, nevertheless, if you do want to keep something of your tone, we can rule it out. I’ve often been tempted to chuck it, but I hold onto it because sometimes its cheap digital allure still appeals to me. The following is not my account of the three pedals that I think all guitarists need, or any nonsense like that. Not at all. Each to their own. If you love flangers and choruses, good for you. This is just about what I feel like I need. And, since I tend to schlep my gear around town by myself, and I don’t drive, I have an interest in minimising how much gear I need to schlep. I don’t use a lot of delay or looping, so the loop station and the delay pedal are hardly close to my heart. So they can go. I do, however, want to extend the range of my guitar way beyond its ‘natural’ range, so the Whammy stays. I don’t really use it for whammy effects, but to play well outside the possible range of the instrument. I love the Whammy. I understand its peculiar timbral ins and outs. Definitely one of my favourite pedals of all time. And since most of my guitars don’t have actual whammies installed, it’s all the more useful. Next, I have a lot of fuzzes and overdrives, and I used to have more. I sold my ProCo Rat, and my old Big Muff PI, and my Boss OD-3, and I gave away my ancient Digitech PDS 1550. If I’m honest, the only one I really adore is the Green Russian Big Muff. Small as it is, it sounds huge, it’s dark, and it fulfils all my fuzz needs. And for reasons which will become apparent, I don’t really need an overdrive. I like the sound of the compressor, as a special effect. But I don’t need it. And since three of my guitars are single-coil-equipped (Strat, Tele, Casino), and it makes them even noisier, that makes it even less essential. So that leaves the tone controls. I don’t play a lot of crazy wah-wah stuff. I like the wah-wah, but having long since got the funky wah-wah moves out of my system, I find myself more and more using it in one random position where it sounds cool. And it’s big, and it’s really heavy. So that just leaves the graphic EQ. Possibly the single most useful pedal I own. I only got it recently. Graphic EQs are absurdly simple. All they do is raise or lower particular frequency bands in your signal. Like all simple and powerful things, they are immensely more useful than they appear to be. This simple pedal not only allows me to completely change the tone of my guitar, it also functions as an overdrive. I’m not sure that even people who know how to properly use a graphic EQ, understand just how ridiculously versatile it is. I’ve seen tons of videos in which guitarists tentatively shift individual faders upwards, and then go Oh yeah, this is handy for shaping your tone. You can do so much more insane shit than that. Not only can you boost individual frequency bands, you can also cut them, making your guitar sound like no guitar that has ever lived. And you can bring up the mids, and not bring up everything else, so it sounds like a wah-wah in a stationary position. And, not content with that, you can also set the faders to neutral and also bring up the overall level, so it works like an overdrive. Also, try putting a fuzzbox in front of this thing and then sculpting the resulting tone with the faders. All of a sudden you have clean tone/clean tone with EQ/fuzztone/fuzztone with EQ. I’m not endorsing any product, but this particular EQ pedal works on frequency bands that are both above and below the natural range of the guitar—which works great for me, with my pitchshifter. So, if I could have only three guitar pedals, it’s easy: the Digitech Whammy, the Green Russian Big Muff, and the Joyo Band Controller. Between them, they do everything that I need pedals to do.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Is modern art (1860–1970) and contemporary art really as bad as the general populace believes?
Answer: I’m not arrogant enough to presume that I know what the ‘general populace’ thinks of the art of the last 160 years. But art in that period did shift from being something that the average person probably found reasonably legible, to something that some supposedly intelligent people profess to find baffling and worthless. The progress of how that happened is beyond my ability to describe in detail, but I think it’s not a coincidence that the beginning of the shift in art away from immediately intelligible, realistic representations of the visible world, coincides with the increasing popularity of photography. In 1838, Louis Daguerre published the first photographic image to depict people. It wasn’t the first photograph ever, but because photographic images in those days required such long exposure times, moving people didn’t stay in one place for long enough to register on them. (Daguerre’s pictures took minutes to expose, but they were still a vast technical improvement on those of his late colleague Niépce, which had taken hours.) However, in the above picture, the guy on the lower left having his shoes shined stayed in one place for long enough for he and his shoeshine guy to appear in the image. I don’t think we can appreciate now what an earthshaking development the first photographs were. For centuries, the visual world had been represented by artists painting and drawing it, and sculptors sculpting it. But now it could be reproduced by a machine. The portrait had once been a luxury item for the rich and powerful, but now anyone could be photographed. This threw the most intelligent artists for a loop. Artistic practice changed. Visual art became an interrogation of representation itself, a process that we can see beginning in the work of e.g. Turner, but the Impressionists really went for it. The line from Impressionism to Cubism is pretty obvious. By WW1, you’ve got an artist like Duchamp rejecting his youthful Cubism and deciding that the point of art is not to please the eye, but to engage the mind. Which is how Duchamp goes from Nude Descending a Staircase, in 1912: —To Fountain, in 1917: Now, the reader may ask: Why? Why couldn’t artists go on painting nice pictures like they used to? Why did they have to start doing things like stick a urinal in a gallery and pretend it’s a sculpture? Why was that necessary? Photography had become the most efficient way of showing what things merely look like. The entire artistic tradition of the female nude, especially when painted by heterosexual male artists, has an element to it that seems to reach its ultimate expression in the far less labour-intensive and far more multiple pornographic photo. I mean, consider François Boucher (1703–1770). There are a lot of different ways to paint nudes, but it would not be controversial to say that Boucher’s female nudes are painted in such a way as to maximise the visual pleasure of the straight male viewer. In Kenneth Clark’s 1956 The Nude: A Study in Ideal Form, Clark talks about Boucher’s The Resting Odalisque in exactly these terms, discussing the painting entirely as if its point was to invite the viewer to ogle its subject, Marie-Louise O’Murphy, one of Louis XV’s mistresses: And Clark says this without any hint of censure. For him, this painting exists for us to ‘take pleasure’ in Miss O’Murphy’s body, and the fact that she’s not looking at us renders her delightfully unselfconscious, which for him is all part of the visual pleasure the picture offers. But there’s another way of looking at it. The picture was commissioned by the French court, and at the time it was painted, Miss O’Murphy was not yet Louis XV’s mistress, but a teenage model affiliated with the Académie royale de peinture et de sculpture, where Boucher taught. The story goes that, when Louis XV saw the picture, he was sufficiently intrigued to want to meet O’Murphy and take her as his mistress. She duly became the youngest of his mistresses, and remained one for a couple of years until she unwisely tried to supplant Madame de Pompadour as the main mistress. She was expelled from court at the age of about 17 (yes, she was younger than that when this picture was painted) and was swiftly married off to a nobleman. She managed to survive three husbands, several pregnancies and the French Revolution, and died in 1814 aged 77. Rather than being an innocent picture of a nude girl, as Clark saw it, this picture can be seen as part of the politico-sexual negotiations of the French court of the Ancién regime: a juicy bauble commissioned and designed to advertise its subject to the monarch, so that he could enjoy her sexual services. The history of the nude in Western art is full of this kind of thing. And artists are, on the whole, no longer willing to play that game—not least because royal courts don’t exactly have in-house painters the way they used to. Artists continue to paint nudes, but the best of them don’t paint nudes the same way that the camera reproduces the appearance of them. I’m thinking of Egon Schiele, and Lucian Freud, and Jenny Saville, and Frank Auerbach, who make the viewer’s encounter with the image much more intimate and ambiguous and raw than it is with the creamy prettiness of Boucher. All along, I’ve been avoiding the question. The reason is that the development of visual art has been such that many people come to the art with an expectation that it’s going to offer them something it has no intention of offering, because the thing that those people want can be had more easily elsewhere. So they think that the art is ‘bad’. A painting like The Resting Odalisque might look, to a certain sort of viewer, simple and easy to enjoy. It’s a lot less simple when you consider the nature of the subject, and the circumstances in which it got made. If you just want to see nice pictures, there are plenty of them to look at. The best modern art is no longer about showing us the world, but about how the artist sees and reproduces it. And that requires a little more effort on the viewer’s part.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Should I watch Guy Ritchie's movie "The Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare"?
Answer: There’s no ‘should’. Watch it if you want. I found it oddly inert. It is my basic belief that Henry Cavill can’t really act, but in this film, he did play the character as written: an unflappable British Chap, who strolls through the movie dealing out death to hapless German mooks with his silenced Sten gun, and quietly improvising on the fly when things don’t go according to plan. I found his character affable and entertaining. Trouble is, the film is basically an excuse to have all its protagonists be variants on that. The team consists of Cavill as the British Chap, then there’s an unflappable Irish Techie (the sailor of the team), and an unflappable Danish Killer, and another unflappable British Chap as the Planner. This one, when we first meet him, is attached by his nipples to a battery because he’s being tortured by the Narzies, but when our team almost effortlessly rescues him, shooting down his torturers as he watches with interest, he then politely and unflappably asks his rescuers to turn off the battery. Then there’s the Unflappable Black SOE Agent (Babs Olusanmokun) and the Unflappable Woman SOE Agent (Eiza Gonzàlez), who IMO is the person in the movie who really can’t act. I am normally the first person to come down hard on complaints that young attractive women can’t act, because the accusation often comes from mere sexism, but Gonzàlez is so wooden that they could have forced German sailors to walk the plank on her. To be fair, English isn’t her native language, and she does sing rather well, I’ll give her that, giving an interesting version of Brecht & Weill’s ‘Moritat’ (‘Mack the Knife’ to you), transposed into E minor to make it sound ominous. Then there’s Rory Kinnear, under a ton of unconvincing makeup, as Winston Churchill, of all people. Possibly the least interesting screen Churchill ever. The only point in the film where Cavill’s character betrays the slightest stress, concern or anxiety is towards the end, regarding a plot point (two characters needing to make a lucky escape under extreme conditions)… which is then simply glossed over, because they suddenly appear, their escape having been left undramatised. Watching this movie made me think idle thoughts about whether or not there’s been a decline in the British WW2 movie. British WW2 movies made during the war, such as The First of the Few, usually emphasised the importance of fighting. In the 50s, the focus shifted, making them films mostly about flawed men dealing with their demons. Ice Cold in Alex is a great example, but so I think is The Cruel Sea, in which some of the main characters are just rubbish, and a lot of them get killed. In the 60s, America was funding most of the war films (The Longest Day, The Bridge at Remagen) and so they’re heavily America-centric, and rely on spectacle and all-star casts. In The Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare, although the plot is very loosely based on a real mission (Operation Postmaster), the movie is an excuse to peddle an image of perfectly calm, competent Britishness. With the Danish guy being sort of honorary British. When the team finds out, two thirds of the way through, that the ship they have trekked to Equatorial Africa to sink has been heavily armoured and is now unsinkable, it takes them about ten seconds of screen time to devise an alternative plan. In a desperate attempt to make them look like they have serious antagonists other than, you know, Nazi Germany, the film constructs Admiral Dudley Pound as a mean, obstructive bureaucrat, determined to stop them. This is not only unfair to Pound, but at this point in the war, Pound was suffering from hip degeneration, the pain of which kept him awake at night, which in turn gave him an unfortunate tendency to doze off in meetings. He would die of a brain tumour a year after the events in this movie, still grieving for his wife, who’d died a few months earlier. Needless to say, Operation Postmaster wasn’t exactly like this. There was an awful lot fewer dozy German soldiers being mowed down by Sten guns, and a lot more prisoner-taking and sneaking about. In short: just another Guy Ritchie movie. Neither a must-see nor an embarrassing shambles. A movie about 2024, not about 1942.

Question: How do I create chords without learning music theory?
Answer: You don’t ‘create’ chords. All the chords have already been created. Every way of voicing them has already been done. You learn how notes in scales are linked together to form chords. This can be done with very little effort. But it involves learning some music theory. Otherwise you’re like the head chef in the kitchen, trying to tell the cooks what to cook, without knowing the names for the foods, or the names of the methods of cooking them. ‘Take the red meat out of the fridge thing, no not that one, the other one, with the bone… no, not the bone in the middle, the bone on the edge… no, not that red meat, are you blind? Right, that one. Now put the white powder and grind the black stuff on it, no wrong white powder, obviously I mean that one… yes, and next, get the red stuff in the bottle and add it to the liquid with the bones, no the other liquid with the bones, no the other liquid with the bones, and put more flame, and… no no no, that liquid with the bones! Pour the red stuff all in there and make it so it goes all steamy and goes less, down to about yay much—‘ ‘Chef, are you asking me to add wine to the veal stock and reduce it to demi-glace?’ ‘DON’T USE THAT COOKING THEORY CRAP IN MY KITCHEN! YOU’RE STIFLING MY CREATIVITY!’

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Who is the most annoying character in the Office?
Answer: Interesting question, but I think I have a solid answer. It’s not Angela. Apologies to anyone who saw Angela’s picture in the preview, and assumed that this answer would be about her. Angela’s great vice is not that she’s judgemental, or hypocritical, or prissy, although she is all those things, at various times. Her great vice, which in season 9 she abjectly owns up to, is pride, which encompasses all those things. Angela thinks she’s ‘virtuous’, but we see from almost her earliest appearances that she isn’t. She’s carrying on a secret thing with Dwight, and apparently she’s rather good at sex. (Which is, of course, not a vice, but from the way Angela talks about other people, you’d think she thinks it is. Dwight describes her as ‘energetic’ and ‘flexible’.) So, from the get-go, Angela is someone whose desire is at odds with her sense of herself—and that’s not annoying, that’s pitiable. Angela’s subconscious longing for a fulfilled life with a good partner is perfectly fine; what’s not fine is her mean-minded sniping about other people who actually have that, because she only snipes about them because she doesn’t have it. Angela’s fortunes slowly decline until, late in season 9, she is genuinely pathetic. Watch her in the scene when her marriage ends, as her gay husband Senator Lipton comes out in a press conference: her reactions are priceless, going from smiling, loyal wife, through disgruntlement, then a look of pure Oh you have to be f***ing kidding me, and finally, when Lipton confesses that he’s really in love with his chief of staff, Angela gasps with disbelief and appears to be about to throw up. (Angela Kinsey, her actor, was wonderful in the role: apparently she’s basically the complete opposite of her character.) A couple of episodes later, she’s dishevelled and dejected, she’s being evicted from her apartment and her beloved cats are being taken away, and she’s sneaking vodka into her giant soft-drink cup. That’s when Oscar, the former lover of her former husband, invites her to stay in his place until she gets her life sorted out. Angela accepts help, almost immediately breaks down and, for the first time in the show, is completely honest with someone else, tearfully confessing to Oscar that she loves Dwight. In the basically humane and compassionate environment of The Office, this is enough to redeem her. From then on, Angela’s fortunes improve. It’s not Dwight, either. Dwight is only superficially annoying. Dwight does not exactly occupy the same moral universe as the rest of us. Dwight lives in a world where he’s the hero of an epic adventure story, in which his least decisions are crucially important. However, to everyone else, including us, Dwight is a paper salesman who also runs a beet farm. So we can’t exactly take Dwight at his word; but, on the other hand, because Dwight adheres so faithfully to his peculiarly archaic and harsh code of ethics (most of the time), there is something oddly noble about him, even at his most idiotic. When things don’t go the way he wants them to, we may well be pleased that some of his more petty and idiotic schemes get defeated; but we might also feel sorry for him, because he is, so often, the architect of his own humiliation. Dwight sets up his own quite stringent standards of failure and success, and at his best, he at least tries to live by them. Which is perhaps why Jim and Pam end up liking him, and consider him a friend. And why, in the end, he considers them as friends—and gives up a dowry that includes a walk-in freezer’s worth of bull semen, because the one he really loves is Angela. Nor is it Jim and/or Pam. They’re relatively normal, funny and sympathetic, unless you’re a dick. So that’s them out. Arguments could be made for a number of other characters. And I might agree with such arguments, as applied to Todd Packer, or Nellie Bertram, or Deangelo Vickers. But I believe I can make a far stronger case for someone else. In my view, the most annoying character in The Office, by far, is Andy Bernard. The enduring feature of Andy’s character, in my view, the one that persists through all his character development and un-development, is his sense of entitlement. It underwrites every aspect of him. Andy tends to coast through life on his first impressions of people, because his smug self-confidence tells him that they’re correct. On Jim’s first day in Stamford, Jim has a tuna sandwich for lunch, so Andy assumes that tuna is Jim’s favourite food, and immediately nicknames him ‘Big Tuna’, although tuna is not Jim’s favourite food. Later on, he assumes that Pam, too, must be sick of eating tuna because, in his mind, Jim wants to eat nothing else. Pam, for her part, is merely baffled. When Jim attempts to prank Andy the way he pranked Dwight, by embedding Andy’s stapler in Jello, it backfires horribly. Dwight got haughty and pompous and made comically unreasonable demands that Jim be fired, which amused Jim no end and which is exactly the kind of thing he expects Andy to do. Instead, Andy epically loses his shit, starts yelling, and kicks a wastebin across the office. And nobody except Jim even raises an eyebrow, because they’re all used to Andy’s explosions of rage when his sense of propriety is violated. When the two branches merge, and Andy comes to Scranton in season 3’s ‘The Merger’, he blithely tells the camera how he plans to gain power: Andy: I'll be the Number Two guy here in Scranton in six weeks. How? Name repetition, personality mirroring, and never breaking off a handshake. I'm always thinking one step ahead. Like a carpenter that makes stairs. Sure enough, this is what Andy does—and it works on Michael, but it doesn’t work on Pam, who sees him doing it to Michael. Check out her silent reactions in the background of the scene where Andy and Michael first meet. We can see that she gets Andy’s number within seconds: Andy: [cautiously] Hello. Michael: Ah! You must be Andy Bernard. Michael: Aloha and welcome! Andy: And you must be Michael Scott. Aloha and... hello. Michael: A-ha-ha-ho. Very good! Welcome to our little kingdom. Ah, we have a bag of nifty gifties for you. Andy: Michael, thank you for welcoming me to your little kingdom, Mike. Michael: Oh. Andy: [looking into the bag] Nifty! Michael: They are nifty! They're nifty gifties. [Cut to Michael in a talking head segment] Michael: You know who I really like, is this guy Andy Bernard. He has got this… very likable way about him. You can watch the whole exchange here. If you’re an obsessive nerd. Andy correctly identifies Dwight as his main ‘rival’ for Number Two Guy in Scranton, and spends the next few episodes not very subtly trying to undermine him, and equally unsubtly trying to get Michael to be his best buddy. Unfortunately for Andy, he does not naturally project warmth, the way Michael does—and indeed, the rather weird way Dwight does. (In Dwight’s case it’s more like ‘fervent heat’.) Andy, when he’s being manipulative, is chilly, and so his attempts to be friendly come across as calculating, and his snide jokes about Dwight come across as bitchy. It doesn’t help that, a few episodes before ‘The Merger’, Dwight had tried and abjectly failed to wrest the management job from Michael, but Michael has already conditionally forgiven him—so he doesn’t need to hear Andy hinting that Dwight can be less than loyal, because he already knows that, but he also wants to think the best of Dwight, and not have some new guy stirring bad blood. In ‘The Return’, a combination of Andy’s last-ditch effort to ingratiate himself with Michael, and Jim’s exasperation with Andy’s mannerisms (such as loudly singing the Cranberries’ ‘Zombie’ at his desk), creates a situation which pushes Andy over the edge. Dwight has been fired (long story), and now works at Staples. Michael notices that Dwight did a lot of little things around the office that made it a nicer place, and is already missing him. Pam points out that Dwight not only watered the plants but arranged the toys on Michael’s desk. Michael: Really? That was very nice of him. We need more attitude like that around the office. Andy: [coming up to them] Feel ya, dawg. Michael: [turning to him] Yeah, do you? Andy: Absolutely. Michael: [hard stare] What did I say? Andy: [who has no idea what Michael was talking about] … You said... [makes gibberish noises] Michael: Huh. Andy: Which is like, "Right on." And Pam was like "blah blah blah" and you were like "Yeah, psht." [smugly] Nailed it. Michael: Oh, no. Andy: [trying and failing to mirror Michael] Oh, no. And now, Michael complains to us that Andy likes him ‘too much’ and is ‘always up in my bidnis.’ The stage is set. Andy has put a ringtone on his phone of himself singing ‘Rockin’ Robin’ in four-part harmony, which he can’t resist showing off. Jim decides to prank him. Pam helps Jim to steal Andy’s phone and hide it in the ceiling above Andy’s desk, and then Pam and Jim take turns to ring it. This, predictably, drives Andy up the wall. Eventually, Michael realises that he has been unjust to Dwight, and that he wants Dwight back. Unfortunately, at this point, an already jittery Andy makes his last attempt to be Michael’s best buddy. It does not go well: Michael: [preparing to go to get Dwight back] Pam, I have a mission to accomplish. Make sure this party gets rolling and I will be back shortly. Andy: Wait up. Where are you going? Do you want me to come with? Michael: Um. Andy: Just listen, I forgot to tell you the plan for this Saturday. You, me, bars, beers, buzzed. Wings. Shots. Drunk. Waitresses, hot. Football: Cornell/Hofstra. Slaughter. Then a quick nap at my place and we'll hit the tiz-own. Michael: [annoyed] No. I don't want to do any of that. Andy: [smarmy] Duh. Which is why I was just joking about doing that. Michael: [snapping] No, just stop. Stop. Stop doing it. You're going to drive me crazy. Andy: [seething] Fine. I'll just sit at my desk and be quiet. Sorry I annoyed you with my friendship. [Andy's phone rings] Excuse me. [to the rest of the office] And I'm also sorry that a lot of people here for some reason think it's funny to steal someone's personal property and hide it from them. Here's a little newsflash! It's not funny! In fact, it's pretty freakin' unfunny! Oh, my GOD! And he punches a hole in the wall. Andy goes off to anger management classes, which he claims he’ll be able to finish in less than the allotted time, and when he comes back he is indeed less angry. However, Andy on his best behaviour is Andy out of focus. He veers between being Michael Lite, Mediocre Jim, or The Guy Angela Got With To Make Dwight Jealous. When he’s not being subjected to routine indignities (like in season 3’s ‘Beach Games’, where he falls into the lake in his sumo suit and spends the rest of the episode drifting helplessly on his back, with everyone ignoring his cries for help), he’s completely failing to see that Angela doesn’t love him. When that’s ended he’s courting Erin, which he does without ever telling Erin that he used to be engaged to Angela. When Erin’s no longer with him and is with Gabe, he drives himself and others nuts trying to win her back—like in season 7’s ‘Viewing Party’, where he ingests large quantities of Gabe’s powdered seahorse in attempt to give himself ‘virility’, and then spends much of the rest of the episode throwing up. Andy only comes back into focus in season 8, where he becomes office manager. Here, he becomes a little more sympathetic because of the trials he’s put through. The best example is ‘The Incentive’, in which he introduces a scheme whereby if the office makes enough sales, he’ll reward them. The top reward is that he’ll let them tattoo whatever they want on his butt. Because Andy isn’t as smart as he thinks he is, he fails to prevent them from pooling their sales, and they quickly make enough sales to meet the target. Andy ruefully but pluckily agrees to go ahead with the butt-tattooing, although I personally think that that the writing team was being soft on his character because it was his turn to be sympathetic—but never mind. He insists on having the tattoo, even though Jim assures him that nobody expects him to, and at the last minute, the office staff take pity on him and switch the tattoo from an insulting one to a picture of a dog with ‘Nard’ written on it, so it’s his old Cornell nickname, ‘Nard Dog’. Andy ends up feeling accepted. But this is one of the few times that Andy lets himself be the butt (!) of the joke. Oh yeah. About the Cornell thing. Andy went to Cornell, one of the Ivy League colleges, and he seldom lets people forget this. Nothing wrong with that. My dad went to Harvard, and even me saying that feels like me ‘doing an Andy’. What matters, though, is not what college you went to, but what you got out of the experience. What Andy got out of it was the sense that he’s better than other people because he went to Cornell. In season 8, Andy decides that he simply has to get back together with Erin, even though he’s engaged to the lovely Jessica. Being Andy, he drives down to Florida to get Erin back, and then breaks up with Jessica on the way home, during her bridal shower. Once he’s got Erin back, the next thing that happens is that his family loses its money and has to sell the family yacht, which he’s never been allowed to captain. Being Andy, he drives with Erin to the harbour, personally commandeers the yacht and sails it to its buyer in the Bahamas, leaving Erin behind. It doesn’t even occur to him to ask her if she’d like to go along, which she admits she would have. He then stays in the Bahamas for three months but doesn’t tell his employers that he’s doing so, leaving the office to run itself (which it does with extreme success). While he’s gone, he tweets continually but only emails his girlfriend twice. On returning, he calmly asks for and accepts all his paychecks and the bonus cheque he hasn’t earned, and then causes Jan to cancel an important sale made in his absence when he annoys her about a minor technical point—the sales team had given her a price they technically weren’t entitled to give her without first clearing it with him, which they couldn’t do, because he was in the Bahamas. Eventually, in season 9, Andy’s love of showbiz trumps his mediocre interest in his job, and, against everyone’s advice, he decides to quit Dunder Mifflin and audition for a reality show. None of the other employees think this a good idea, but the truest and most withering verdict comes from Phyllis: Phyllis: Andy sings beautifully. And he's really good at dancing. He's a good speaker. But there's just something there you don't want to look at. Sure enough, after pointlessly taking a dump on David Wallace’s car (so as to ‘burn my bridges’), Andy barges into a young girl’s audition and starts belting out the ‘Cornell Fight Song’ before finally collapsing before the pitiless unenthusiasm of the judges, and bursting into self-pitying tears. In the end, unable to function in the regular world, Andy gets to retreat to his beloved Cornell. Which he probably should never have left. Andy is annoying partly because privileged people shouldn’t be so f***ing clueless. He should know better. With his preppy background and his Ivy League education, you’d think Andy would at least have more manners, but his sense of manners is confined to pointless instructions about how to eat food at his disastrous garden party (which the others have to rescue for him: when the gang are all relaxing at the end, and Darryl is cooking on the grill which Andy specifically told him not to bring, Darryl offers Andy a cheeseburger, and Andy finally relaxes, instead of yearning after the approval of his asshole father). When he was making an effort to be a better man, he did become more genuinely friendly and helpful. But there’s something queasily inauthentic about him: some part of him that is always pretending. Michael Scott needs to be liked. Dwight doesn’t care whether he’s liked. Angela just doesn’t like people. Kevin rather endearingly assumes that he is liked. Jim and Pam and Darryl are naturally likeable. But Andy thinks he deserves to be liked, and that if people refuse to like him, he can make them like him by tricks and hacks, and when they fail, by plain old sucking up. When he is thwarted, he typically reacts by either exploding with rage or bursting into tears. In the end, once he had the job he wanted, the real Andy had to re-emerge. Privilege let him be his truest self: convinced he had the right to be the boss, but only barely competent as one, and fatally too uninterested be a good one. It also has something to do with Ed Helms’ tight smirk and narrow, wary eyes, and Andy’s slightly too-loud voice, and irritating hamminess, such as his fondness for fake Cockney accents. I know, I know, it’s subjective. Some people probably find Andy endearing. An unloved child, fretting in the shadow of his handsomer, more talented brother (who is after all Josh Groban.) But to me, Andy is the character you most enjoy getting punched. Like Phyllis said: there’s just something there you don’t want to look at.

Question: What can I make with flour, eggs, salt, water and olive oil?
Answer: You can make a simple flatbread with the flour, salt, water and olive oil, and you can fry the eggs and dip the flatbread into it. Here’s a simple flatbread recipe which I’ve made, so I can assure you that it works: Make the dough, then fry the flatbreads and keep them warm while you fry a couple of eggs in very hot olive oil. I suggest searingly hot olive oil, for sixty seconds each, so they’re crispy on the outside but still have liquid yolks. It would be nice to have some raw vegetables with this, or salad, but when we’re poor, we’re poor, and the contrast between the crispy/doughy flatbread and the fried eggs is very pleasant. A few leaves, if possible a squeeze of lemon or some vinegar, and some cheap wine, would make this into a feast.

Question: What is one of the best comedy movies you've watched recently?
Answer: I watched one this weekend which I heartily endorse, Bottoms, a 2023 movie by Canadian director Emma Seligman. L to r: Rachel Sennott, Ruby Cruz, Ayo Edebiri Bottoms was succinctly described by my daughter as ‘Booksmart meets Fight Club except they’re both lesbians.’ It concerns two high school students, P.J. (Sennott, who co-wrote the script with Seligman) and Josie (Edebiri), who are known in their school as the ‘ugly untalented gays’, and by ‘known in their school’ I mean that when the principal wants to see them, he announces over the intercom ‘Could the ugly untalented gays please report to the principal’s office.’ P.J. and Josie, who are best friends, are each pining with forlorn love for two popular cheerleaders, Brittany and Isabel. At the start of the film, they’re attending a fair with their rather dorky friend Hazel (Cruz) when they witness Isabel having a fight with her boyfriend Jeff, captain of the school football team. They invite Isabel to have a ride home in their car, and as Jeff stands in front of the car and shouts at Isabel, the car rolls forward slightly and gently touches Jeff’s knees, causing him to collapse on the ground screaming in agony. This incident gets turned by the school rumour mill into a rumour that P.J. and Josie were in juvie over summer break, and physically fought with Jeff. Eager to seem cooler than they are, they both play up to this rumour: Josie: Juvie was insane. Once, a girl tried to kill me with rat poison so I took her outside and I punched her 'til she died. In order to avoid expulsion, the girls persuade the principal that they were setting up a self-defence club, which they proceed to do, so that they can get attractive girls to sleep with them. They manage to persuade their history teacher, Mr. G (Marshawn Lynch), to endorse them. Soon, they and a bunch of other girls, including Hazel, are enthusiastically beating each other up in the school gymnasium. I won’t spoil the plot by telling any more, but this is a fabulously weird school comedy that feels like it was made in the 90s by time travellers, because no 90s film would have these two particular protagonists. P.J. is the aggressive, sweary, motormouth one and Josie is the mild-mannered one who tags along with P.J.’s harebrained schemes, so of course there’s a moment where their friendship breaks down and Josie explodes at P.J. about what an idiot she is. Marshawn Lynch was, I gather, a football player, but he has excellent comedy chops as the rather idiotic but basically benign Mr. G. The only actor in this that I knew from anything else is Punkie Johnson as P.J. and Josie’s former babysitter and lesbian role model, Rhodes, who lives out of a trailer, swigs whiskey and fruit juice, and has little in the way of sage life advice, but does deliver to Josie some crucial plot information. Followed by some incomprehensible mumbling, to which the ever-earnest Josie replies, ‘I didn’t understand a word of that, I’m so sorry.’ One amusing detail is that Jeff and his fellow teammates are always wearing their football kit, even in the cafeteria or at weekends. The homoerotic subtext of football is here full-blown text: Jeff himself may not be gay (he’s having an affair with Hazel’s mom, and after they’ve had sex he asks Mrs Callahan, can I have a snack?) but his best friend and teammate Tim clearly crushes on him. My favourite character is Hazel, who does a lot of the admin of setting up the club and whose favourite solution to any major problem is to plant a bomb (P.J.: Yeah, Hazel, let’s do terrorism.) She makes and deploys quite a few bombs in the course of the film, but they seldom go off exactly when she wants them to. In one of the most dramatic scenes, the efficacy of the self-defence club is tested when Tim maliciously makes Hazel fight the school’s champion wrestler, Tucker, who is about twice her size. Poor Hazel holds her own for a while but ultimately gets the crap viciously kicked out of her, one of the events that serves to tear the whole situation apart at the end of act two. Still, this is a comedy, so the fun lies in seeing how in the world everything can possibly be fixed by the end. (This is a film which averts the TV trope ‘Beauty is Never Tarnished’: early on, Josie punches P.J. and P.J. sports a nose plaster and two black eyes for the next twenty minutes.) I was wondering why I hadn’t even heard of this movie and my daughter said ‘It’s because its demographic is teenage girls.’ Well, maybe, but I think everyone needs to see it. Okay, maybe not ‘needs to’, but I would have liked to be told P.J. and Josie’s story as a teenage boy. Young men can never have too many heroines, and the final climactic football match features some truly over-the-top mayhem. Some of it involving a sword. If you fancy a lesbian misfit high school comedy with genuinely painful-looking violence in it, this movie is the one for you.

Question: Is there a word or a phrase to describe someone that force themselves to watch or listen to boring pretentious films or music?
Answer: Do you know anyone who does that? I mean, people who force themselves to watch films or listen to music which they themselves consider boring or pretentious? Or just people who force themselves to watch films or listen to music which you consider boring or pretentious? Because if it’s the latter, has it occurred to you that maybe they don’t find it boring or pretentious, but… actually like it? Another answer just says ‘Critic’, and it’s true that critics, unlike the rest of us, are sometimes obliged to endure films and music that they don’t like. I did slightly know a film reviewer, some years ago, who seemed to specialise in the most forbidding kind of obscure arthouse cinema. He would frequently praise such films by saying something like In this film, [X] does not indulge in the cheap satisfactions of Hollywood conventions of narrative ‘pace’, but continually and bracingly challenges the lazy viewer’s patience by static shots of up to ten minutes and a refusal to pander to audience expectations, which from context usually meant This film has no story. I actually like a lot of so-called ‘arthouse’ cinema, but I never understood the tactic of praising a film by saying, in essence, This film is plotless, frustrating and impenetrable but, see, that’s actually what’s good about it. In the meantime: is this a question about people you know, or is it a question about films and music you don’t like?

Question: What do Americans hate the most about America?
Answer: Allow me to present the testimony of one eminent American. Frank Zappa. The documentary Eat That Question: Frank Zappa In His Own Words features an interview with Zappa from I think the late 70s or early 80s, in which he says the following (my transcription but you’re welcome to look it up): The thing that sets the Americans apart from the rest of the cultures in the world is, we’re so fucking stupid. This country’s been around for a couple of hundred years and we think we’re hot shit. And— and we don’t even realise that the other countries have thousands of years of history and culture. And they’re proud of it. And when we deal, on an international level, with, uh, foreign policy and stuff like that, we try to go in and say ‘Oh, big American, strong country’ and all that stuff, they must laugh up their sleeves at us, because we are nothing. We’re culturally nothing. We mean nothing. We’re only interested in the bottom line. Y’know… every other country has their own art, their own music, their own theater, their own drama, their folk dances, folk songs, folk lore. It means something to them, they’re proud of it and that’s their ethnic heritage. We have Levi’s, we have designer jeans, we have hamburgers, we have Coca-Cola, we have REO Speedwagon, we have Journey, we have this one and we have that one and then we go out there and we say ‘Yeah, but we also have neutron bombs and poison gas, so maybe that makes up for it.’ I mean… it’s really kinda sad, when you evaluate it that way. And I think that a country that doesn't do something to sustain its culture, whatever it is, doesn’t invest in it, doesn’t keep it happening, isn’t proud of it… maybe they just shouldn’t exist. Because it’s the culture, the beautiful things that society produces, those are the things that should survive for thousands of years. Not the designer jeans.

Question: Why do MAGAS use words like socialism or communism without having any idea what they mean?
Answer: It makes them feel like they’re doing something out of principle. Because that’s a lot more comforting than the reality. Donald Trump has always been only about one thing: Donald Trump. He is a grifter; a scammer. The product is irrelevant, whether it’s real estate, or shitty vodka, or bad steaks, or a fake university, or just himself-as-president. He sells people confidence in him. Thing is, the con man is an American archetype, a product of a young country expanding, and needing promises to keep going. So he’s tapping into something deep in the American psyche. Along with the need for, not collective effort, but The Man to come along, who will sort everything out. But MAGAts are not noted for their reading of Constance Rourke’s American Humor or Melville’s The Confidence-Man. So Trump, with the certainty of a sleepwalker—because he’s no stable genius—tapped into another American archetype: fear of foreign influence. Socialism and communism are perceived as being dangerously foreign and subversive, the machinations of suspiciously bearded European types, as well as, yunno, Jews and homeysexuals. Not at all the plain common sense of good solid honourable white Christian folk. And there’s another strong strain in American culture: mistrust of the gubmint. Socialism and communism are when the gubmint does stuff! Everyone knows that! Just like the gubmint freed great-grandpappy’s slaves all those years ago! They were much happier when they were slaves! ‘Twas socialisticness and communismals freed the slaves, so that the Marxist adulterer Martin Luther King could et cetera et cetera! Fortunately, my trusty AR-15 will take out the gubmint redcoats, as they march in single file up the road to try to take my guns away. It worked in 1776 and it’ll work now. Anyway, when we make abortion illegal it ain’t the gubmint doing it: it’s just decent people doing what’s right. When we ban the woke BLM Marxists from teaching anti-white pedophilia to kindergarten kids, it ain’t the gubmint, it’s just common sense. Never mind what’s actually going on, I know, because someone told me. When we change the law to make it compulsory to have prayer in schools, it ain’t the gubmint, it’s making the country into the white, Christian nation it was supposed to have been all along. I know that because someone on YouTube told me. Donald Trump got into politics not because he wanted to serve the public, but to boost his brand. In doing so, he tapped into existing strains of racism, anti-intellectualism, homophobia and bigotry in American life, in which two of the reigning demons are ‘socialism’ and ‘communism’. They have nothing to do with actual socialism and communism: they just stand for something that his supporters feel they have to be terrified of. Because it’s more comforting than I voted for this man so he could stay rich. That’s Trump’s ultimate appeal: he amplifies and magnifies his supporters’ existing worst fears, then pretends that only he can stand in the way of them. But the time never comes when he has to. He will defeat the demons… when they show up. Which will be soon. You’re gonna hear something and it will be big. We have all the facts. It’s the worst thing that was ever done. You’ll be hearing all about it. Soon. So, first of all, let me assert my firm belief that the only thing we have to fear is... fear itself — nameless, unreasoning, unjustified terror which paralyzes needed efforts to convert retreat into advance. In every dark hour of our national life, a leadership of frankness and of vigor has met with that understanding and support of the people themselves which is essential to victory. And I am convinced that you will again give that support to leadership in these critical days. —Franklin D. Roosevelt

Question: What are the best songs by R.E.M.?
Answer: Well, these are my favourites, anyway, so I think they’re the best. The boys in 1991, kings of the world: Bill Berry, Peter Buck, Mike Mills in ‘suddenly handsome’ mode, Michael Stipe. R.E.M. were, I think, inseparable from their time and place, for a lot of us who were/are fans of them. Their early songs was self-consciously incomprehensible. Their very earliest songs, as captured on bootlegs and rehearsal tapes, were simple boy-girl garage rock ditties, but at some point they decided that if they were ever going to get anywhere, they needed some extra ingredient, and that extra ingredient was contributed largely by singer/lyricist Michael Stipe: mystery. Stipe went from coherently bawling simple lyrics to mumbling enigmatic lyrics, or stretching out vowels and swallowing consonants so that even when he could be heard, you had little idea what he was singing. Large stretches of their debut album are, as a result, impossible to decipher. When you’re a confused adolescent, as so many of us were in the 80s, this meant that you could project whatever meaning you wanted onto their songs, and pesky things like clear interpretations wouldn’t get in the way. Eddie Vedder of Pearl Jam put this superbly well when he inducted them into the RRHOF in 2007: And, how do you explain the dialogue between Michael and the listener—a dialogue that grew up and we grew up with it? Uh, such wisdom in the feelings in these songs that, I think, they helped us find things that we knew were inside us, and I think they helped us find things that we didn’t know we had inside us. And I can say, there are things that I hold and feel [hand on heart] very deeply about inside here, that Michael Stipe put in there himself. What’s really incredible about this is, is that while this is happening… this all happens without ever being able to understand a fucking word he is saying. And while the songs were incomprehensible, the music of those songs was always direct, appealing, and a strange combination of 60s nostalgia and 70s new wave: energetic enough to be stirring, but familiar enough to feel comforting. Back in the day, they used to get endless comparisons to the Byrds, but there was always as much Soft Boys and Television and Patti Smith in the mix. This is what made them so appealing, when you’re young. But as we grew older, they maybe started to seem less like something that we needed. Stipe couldn’t go on singing like that forever. He had opinions—righteous ones, to be sure—and he wanted to share them. In song form. Which wasn’t always 100% effective. Their music became less elusive and more direct. They became huge with a song like ‘Everybody Hurts’, which I thought was so on-the-nose that it was silly, but some people loved it. Then they took stylistic turns which sometimes thrilled me, but which displeased many of the fans they’d gained by becoming world-famous. I thought Monster was a sleazy, sardonic, noisy, surprisingly tender masterpiece, but it turned off the people who wanted more ‘Everybody Hurts’. By the time I was in my late 20s, they were still going, and getting new audiences, but I was no longer in love with them. (And, believe me, I had a serious and very confusing Stipe crush when I was 16 or so, and too lacking in self-knowledge to realise that I had one.) And then Bill Berry left, and they kept going. I bought Up out of loyalty, but it made me sad, and I couldn’t tell if it made me sad because the songs were sad, or because the band made me sad by no longer being what they had once been to me. (I suspect now it was both.) And after that, I lost touch with them. I didn’t even listen to their last three albums until after they’d broken up, years later. But I have at least listened to all their stuff. And I salute them, on behalf of all of us who were helped through difficult adolescences by their music. In no particular order, then:

Question: Whats the very first thing as a beginner to learn on my Gibson Les Epiphone Special 2 guitar and is it wise to go ahead and switch my pickups out?
Answer: The very first thing to learn is What are all the different sounds I can get out of my guitar? (‘Gibson Les Epiphone’? I think you’re confused about the name.) If you can’t get your guitar to sound the way that you want it to sound as-is, the painful but obvious conclusion is that you bought the wrong guitar for you. You’re in no position yet to judge whether it needs different pickups. You’ve got to take it round the block a few times first. I never liked the neck pickup on my Telecaster, but I nevertheless waited about ten years before actually changing it. As for what you should learn to play, I am firmly of the opinion that those who aren’t taking formal lessons should start by learning to play whatever they most want to play, because they’ll be more motivated to practice it. If you are taking formal lessons, it’s more up to your teacher to decide what you should start with. Personally, I started playing blues straight away and went on from there. I don’t regret that. I regret not learning to improve my reading skills sooner, but I never wasted time trying to learn things just because I thought I ought to but didn’t want to.

Question: What was something a teacher or professor did that made you say "let’s drop this class immediately."?
Answer: Well, I didn’t actually drop the class, because I needed the credit, but I did stop trusting the teacher. I was in a Technology of Music tutorial. Our tutor was a physics lecturer who sang in a choir in his spare time. He was very good about things like the inverse square law and the Sabine equation, and I lapped all that stuff up. However, his grasp of music history was… less certain. He was talking about piano manufacture and construction, and he got onto the subject of John Cage’s music for prepared piano. Cage would ‘prepare’ pianos by placing objects on and between the strings, to make them sound different. I have the score of his Sonatas and Interludes for Prepared Piano and there’s a big table on p. 5 telling the performer what to put where on the strings, so as to get the effect Cage desired: However, our tutor told us about Cage preparing pianos, and then said with a combination of amazement and horror at human folly, And Cage used to drive nails into pianos, and screw bolts into them! He physically destroyed perfectly good pianos, doing this! Shocked murmurs from some of the other students. Well, I knew Cage’s career pretty well, and I was startled, too much so to raise my hand and say Uh, sorry, but that’s completely untrue. I actually wondered if he might be right. Once I was home I looked it up, and there is zero evidence of Cage ever damaging pianos with his preparations. But after that, while I listened to our tutor when he was talking about science, I never trusted him again when he was discussing music history.
